lessons.title: Part III — offshore instruction
lessons.body: # Part III — offshore instruction

lessons.title: O01 — Preparing for an offshore assignment
lessons.body:
## O01 — Preparing for an offshore assignment

### Objectives

Prepare a travel and personal-readiness plan; distinguish identification, access permission and task qualification; resolve fatigue, medication and extended-stay concerns before boarding.

An offshore assignment starts before departure. A worker who arrives at the shorebase without the correct documents, too fatigued to follow a briefing, or without an adequate supply of necessary medication has a work-planning problem, not merely a personal inconvenience. Distance, transport schedules and weather can delay access to ordinary support. Preparation makes those limitations visible while they can still be addressed.

Confirm the destination, reporting time, dispatcher contact, transport mode and baggage arrangements with your employer. Ask which identification, operator-accepted orientation, medical clearance and task qualifications are required for your particular assignment. These are different records. A general safety course does not establish medical fitness or authorization to operate equipment. A maritime access credential does not prove completion of a site induction. Check names, dates and the method used to verify records before travel rather than asking the dispatcher to resolve everything at boarding.

Plan the journey so you can arrive rested. Driving through the night and then starting a demanding shift makes the journey part of the exposure. Tell the responsible supervisor when delays or an extended previous shift undermine the plan. Stop safely before consulting navigation or communicating a route change. Do not try to recover lost time by speeding. The useful question is whether the revised journey and work schedule remain safe, not whether the original arrival time can still be reached.

Use the employer's confidential process for medication and fitness questions. Prescription ownership, correct use and fitness for a particular duty are separate issues. An over-the-counter product can affect alertness; a prescribed product can also require review. Keep medication in its identified container and follow the relevant travel and company requirements. Do not take another person's medication or stop a prescribed treatment merely to pass a work check. Consult the appropriate healthcare professional and employer fitness contact about safe arrangements. Share necessary fitness restrictions through the designated channel rather than broadcasting medical details to coworkers.

Prepare for a delayed return. Arrange essential home responsibilities, sufficient permitted personal supplies and a way to contact the appropriate family or support person. Confirm how the employer handles weather extensions and medication shortages. A backup plan is not a promise that a worker will remain offshore indefinitely. If an essential need cannot be met, report it early so the responsible people can change the travel or assignment plan.

Check prohibited-item rules before packing. Weapons, ammunition, alcohol, illegal drugs, ignition sources and other restricted articles may be controlled by the facility or carrier. Never assume an item allowed in a private vehicle is permitted in baggage or on a helicopter. Declare uncertainty before entering a controlled area. Security staff, not a coworker's informal assurance, resolve an access issue.

### Worked situation

Mara has a current orientation record but has driven seven hours after a night shift. Her flight is delayed, and she has only enough prescribed medicine for the planned return date. She proposes boarding first and sorting the details out offshore. The appropriate action is to tell dispatch and her supervisor about the fatigue and supply problem before departure, use the confidential fitness channel, and obtain a revised plan. Her orientation record does not remove either limitation. The error would be concealing the problem to avoid missing transport; that removes the opportunity to arrange a safe alternative.

### Practice and explained response

List the separate decisions in Mara's situation. A complete response identifies transport eligibility, present fitness, medication continuity and work scheduling. The learner should name the responsible contacts and state that a travel booking alone resolves none of these decisions. If the response is only “get more sleep,” revisit how travel, duty and delayed return interact.



### Learning checks

#### O01-L1

Your return may be delayed by weather, but your medication supply ends on the planned return day. What is the best next step?

A. Board and request an early flight later

B. Resolve supply and fitness arrangements through the proper contacts before departure

C. Borrow the same-looking medicine from a coworker

D. Stop taking it during the trip

#### O01-L2

Which statement correctly distinguishes an orientation record from work readiness?

A. The record authorizes every task mentioned in the course

B. A transport booking substitutes for any missing qualification

C. Fitness, access and task authorization still need their own applicable checks

D. A supervisor can ignore fatigue when the record is current

#### O01-L3

You will arrive after an overnight drive immediately following a long shift. What should change?

A. Tell the supervisor and revise travel or duty arrangements before the exposure

B. Drive faster to create a short rest period

C. Avoid reporting fatigue unless you fall asleep

D. Use another worker’s stimulant medication

### Explained answers and remediation

**O01-L1: Resolve supply and fitness arrangements through the proper contacts before departure** A delayed return is foreseeable. Resolve continuity and fitness through the clinician and employer process; do not borrow medication or change treatment to fit transport. Reread O01 and explain the corrected action using the chapter practice.

**O01-L2: Fitness, access and task authorization still need their own applicable checks** Orientation is one component. It does not establish fitness, access permission or competence for a specialist task. Reread O01 and explain the corrected action using the chapter practice.

**O01-L3: Tell the supervisor and revise travel or duty arrangements before the exposure** Fatigue belongs in the journey and work plan. Reporting it early allows rest or a revised assignment instead of concealing the exposure. Reread O01 and explain the corrected action using the chapter practice.

lessons.title: O02 — Shorebase arrival, security and accountability
lessons.body:
## O02 — Shorebase arrival, security and accountability

### Objectives

Use the authorized access process; explain maritime security levels; correct manifest discrepancies; maintain accountability from the shorebase to the offshore destination.

A shorebase combines passenger movements, freight handling, traffic and controlled access. Arriving at the right address does not mean every route through the property is open to you. Park where directed, secure the vehicle, report to the named dispatcher or security contact, and stay within the permitted waiting area. Read the local instructions rather than following a group that may have a different destination or permission.

For covered maritime secure areas, a Transportation Worker Identification Credential concerns access screening. The facility or vessel controls actual entry. Where an authorized escort arrangement is available, follow that arrangement; do not assume an escort must be offered. A person with a valid card can still be denied a particular area or directed to remain with an escort. Never lend an access card, follow closely through a controlled door, or treat a familiar uniform as proof of authorization. Resolve missing or expired documentation through security before entry.

MARSEC is a maritime-security alert framework. Level 1 maintains baseline protective measures. Level 2 adds protection for heightened risk. Level 3 applies further specific measures when an incident is probable, imminent or has occurred. Workers do not select the level themselves. Follow the current facility instructions, which can change screening, waiting locations or movement permissions. Do not photograph or publicize sensitive access arrangements to explain a delay. Report a suspicious item or behavior to the designated security contact without investigating it yourself.

The passenger manifest is an accountability record. Confirm your identity, destination and any required passenger or baggage information through the carrier's process. Do not understate weights, move baggage between people to conceal a limit, or change seats when seating is assigned for loading or emergency arrangements. A spelling discrepancy is worth resolving before departure because an emergency team may depend on that record. Notify dispatch if you miss a movement or transfer to another authorized transport; an unchanged manifest can leave rescuers looking in the wrong place.

Attend the transport briefing even if you have travelled before. The vessel, aircraft, exits, flotation equipment, route and conditions may differ. Tell the crew before departure if you cannot hear, understand or physically perform the required passenger action. Ask for a demonstration or other understandable instruction. Nodding through an unintelligible briefing does not make a passenger prepared.

Stay clear of freight operations while waiting. Suspended loads, reversing equipment and mooring activity can cross what looks like an empty walkway. Use designated pedestrian routes, respect barriers and obtain positive direction when the route changes. Do not move a barrier or duck beneath a load to reach a boarding group. Report the conflict so the movements can be separated.

### Worked situation

The manifest lists Jon for Platform East, but his supervisor's message says Platform West. A coworker suggests boarding because both are “nearby.” Jon stays in the designated waiting area and asks dispatch to reconcile the destination with the supervisor. He does not simply amend a paper list himself or board a different craft. A wrong destination can break both work authorization and emergency accountability.

### Practice and explained response

Security announces additional screening while a worker insists that a valid access card means immediate entry. Explain the error. The card is one part of access control; current facility security instructions still apply. The appropriate response is to follow screening and contact the authorized security representative about the delay, not evade the line or borrow another entrance.



### Learning checks

#### O02-L1

Your maritime access card is valid, but security requires an escort. What should you do?

A. Enter alone because the card is current

B. Ask another passenger to lend an unrestricted badge

C. Use an unstaffed gate

D. Follow the facility’s authorized access arrangement

#### O02-L2

The manifest lists a different destination from your assignment. What is the correct response?

A. Board and ask the pilot to change destination

B. Have dispatch reconcile the record before boarding

C. Cross out the destination without informing anyone

D. Follow the largest group of passengers

#### O02-L3

A higher MARSEC level changes the boarding process. What does that mean for a worker?

A. Security is optional for familiar workers

B. The worker should choose a lower level

C. Follow the additional facility measures and use security contacts for questions

D. It authorizes passengers to investigate suspicious objects

### Explained answers and remediation

**O02-L1: Follow the facility’s authorized access arrangement** The credential does not override facility access controls. Security determines the permitted arrangement. Reread O02 and explain the corrected action using the chapter practice.

**O02-L2: Have dispatch reconcile the record before boarding** Dispatch and the responsible assignment contact must reconcile the destination. Accurate manifests support transport planning and accountability. Reread O02 and explain the corrected action using the chapter practice.

**O02-L3: Follow the additional facility measures and use security contacts for questions** MARSEC changes protective measures. Workers follow the current instructions rather than bypass controls or investigate threats themselves. Reread O02 and explain the corrected action using the chapter practice.

lessons.title: O03 — Helicopter travel and helideck awareness
lessons.body:
## O03 — Helicopter travel and helideck awareness

### Objectives

Identify passenger hazards around a helicopter; use the crew's briefing and loading instructions; distinguish ordinary passenger preparation from specialist underwater-escape training.

Rotor movement, noise, wind and constrained deck space make a helicopter different from a car with overhead blades. The safest passenger movement is the one directed by the flight or helideck crew for that aircraft and location. Remain in the designated waiting place until directed. Do not infer permission from an open door, another passenger's movement, or your previous trip.

Before entering the movement area, secure loose belongings and follow instructions for baggage, headwear, eye and hearing protection, and clothing. A loose article can become a distraction or an airborne hazard. Do not chase a dropped item toward an aircraft or over the deck edge. Stop in a safe location, alert the crew, and let them control recovery. Keep long objects and baggage in the manner the crew specifies; do not lift them overhead. Never walk toward the tail or choose an unbriefed route around the aircraft.

Provide accurate information for the passenger and baggage loading process. Aircraft loading concerns both total load and its distribution. An apparently small unreported item or unauthorized seat change can defeat that plan. Let the crew handle loading limits and seating; passengers do not calculate an exception or trade places informally. Report a seatbelt or seat problem before movement rather than improvising a restraint.

In the briefing, locate your restraint, normal exit and the emergency arrangements relevant to your seat. Understand who directs door operation, how instructions will be communicated, and what passenger safety equipment is provided. Ask the crew to resolve a point you do not understand. Do not touch aircraft controls or open doors except as instructed. During a critical phase, avoid distracting the crew; communicate an urgent safety problem using the briefed method.

Overwater equipment is aircraft- and operation-specific. The briefing and required specialist training establish how to use the provided flotation or breathing equipment and when to act. This written orientation cannot replace a supervised helicopter underwater-escape or water-survival course. It deliberately does not teach a universal ditching sequence: seat orientation, exits, restraints and equipment differ. Before accepting an assignment, confirm that any required transport survival training is current and accepted by the operator.

Arrival still requires direction. Stay secured until the crew authorizes the next movement. Leave by the designated route, maintain the instructed clearance and go to the identified safe area. The helideck can have simultaneous freight or fuel activity, weather exposure and limited escape paths. Do not stop for photographs or stand in a route while searching your bag. If the deck is wet or moving, follow the crew's movement instructions and report any inability to proceed safely.

### Worked situation

A passenger's cap blows away as the group approaches a helicopter. The passenger turns toward the tail to retrieve it. The safe response is to stop the unsafe movement from a safe position and alert the crew. Another passenger should not run after the person through the same hazard. Recovering property is secondary to keeping everyone in the controlled passenger route.

### Practice and explained response

A coworker offers to demonstrate emergency exit operation using a method learned on another helicopter type. Explain why you should use the current crew's briefing instead. The aircraft and exit can differ; unapproved practice may damage equipment or create confusion. Ask the crew for the correct demonstration and complete any required specialist training before transport.



### Learning checks

#### O03-L1

A loose article blows toward the helicopter tail. What should a passenger do?

A. Remain safe and alert the crew instead of chasing it

B. Run low beneath the tail

C. Ask another passenger to retrieve it immediately

D. Reach around the tail while holding a rail

#### O03-L2

Why must a passenger report baggage and weight information accurately?

A. Only to calculate baggage fees

B. To decide who boards first

C. Only so the employer can track luggage

D. The crew uses loading information for aircraft limits and distribution

#### O03-L3

A briefing is hard to hear and the aircraft differs from your previous trip. What should happen?

A. Use the previous aircraft’s exit procedure

B. Ask for understandable instruction before departure

C. Wait until an emergency to ask

D. Assume another passenger will explain later

### Explained answers and remediation

**O03-L1: Remain safe and alert the crew instead of chasing it** Property recovery must not draw a passenger into rotor hazards. The crew controls recovery and passenger movement. Reread O03 and explain the corrected action using the chapter practice.

**O03-L2: The crew uses loading information for aircraft limits and distribution** Loading is a safety calculation under crew control. Concealed baggage or informal seat changes can invalidate the arrangement. Reread O03 and explain the corrected action using the chapter practice.

**O03-L3: Ask for understandable instruction before departure** The current aircraft and equipment matter. Resolve comprehension before flight; previous travel is not a substitute. Reread O03 and explain the corrected action using the chapter practice.

lessons.title: O04 — Vessel travel and personnel transfers
lessons.body:
## O04 — Vessel travel and personnel transfers

### Objectives

Recognize vessel-motion and transfer hazards; follow the master and transfer crew; identify conditions requiring a hold; explain why this course does not qualify transfer operators.

A vessel and an offshore structure may move differently. A gap that looks manageable can change while a passenger is committed to crossing it. Slippery surfaces, wind, wake, hand injuries and loose baggage add to the exposure. Do not choose your own transfer method or timing. The authorized transfer team determines whether conditions, equipment and personnel are suitable.

Before boarding, receive the vessel briefing and identify the passenger area, alarms, muster location and relevant emergency responsibilities. Locate the instructions or station bill provided by the crew. Make sure the manifest reflects your presence. Wear the specified personal flotation and other protective equipment as instructed; ask the crew to correct fit or a defect before transfer. A carried flotation device is not the same as one correctly worn when required. Do not substitute an unapproved item because it is more comfortable.

Use only the designated boarding arrangement when released by the crew. Keep hands away from surfaces that can close together, moving lines and unguarded edges. Do not use mooring lines as handholds or stand inside loops of line. Keep baggage under the crew's arrangement so it does not block your view or occupy hands needed for safe movement. If the route, handhold or footing is unclear, ask before committing to the transfer. Do not jump a gap or attempt a transfer because the person ahead succeeded.

During transit, remain in permitted areas, secure belongings and use the handholds or seating arrangements provided. Report illness or impairment early. Seasickness can reduce the ability to follow instructions; hiding it until transfer leaves fewer options. Never lean beyond a rail to retrieve property, dispose of waste or obtain a better view. A person overboard requires an immediate alarm and the vessel's response, not an untrained passenger entering the water.

Personnel transfer devices require equipment-specific instruction and a controlled operation. Designs vary: a method suitable for one device may be unsafe on another. Before use, the transfer team must brief the passenger's position, restraints or handholds, baggage rules, signals and response to an aborted transfer. The designated crew handles equipment inspection, crane operation and transfer authorization. Passengers must report a defect or inability to follow the method, rather than treating a current orientation certificate as competence to rig or operate the system.

If communication is lost, weather changes, a passenger becomes unwell, or the landing area is obstructed, report it immediately and follow the crew's hold or abort instruction. Do not improvise signals. Schedule pressure is not a control for vessel motion. An incomplete transfer can mean remaining offshore or returning ashore under a revised plan; it does not justify self-directed climbing or jumping.

### Worked situation

A supply vessel arrives after dark. A waiting worker sees the platform crew wave but cannot tell whether the signal is directed at passengers or cargo handlers. The worker remains in the designated safe place and asks the passenger-transfer lead for a clear release. A general wave is not a substitute for the agreed signal. The delay prevents a person from entering a cargo movement or a transfer not ready for passengers.

### Practice and explained response

Identify three reasons to request a transfer hold. Suitable answers include an obstructed landing area, unclear communications, defective passenger equipment, or inability to follow the briefing. The learner must describe reporting the condition to the transfer lead and awaiting direction, not personally declaring the entire operation safe after a quick glance.



### Learning checks

#### O04-L1

You cannot tell whether a wave from the platform is a passenger-transfer signal. What should you do?

A. Treat any wave as clearance

B. Follow the next passenger quickly

C. Wait in the safe area and obtain the agreed clear instruction

D. Invent a return signal

#### O04-L2

Which is a reason to request a transfer hold?

A. The landing area is obstructed

B. The shift is running late

C. Another person has transferred successfully

D. The destination is familiar

#### O04-L3

What does this orientation authorize you to do with a personnel-transfer device?

A. Operate the crane after observing one lift

B. Choose the device’s rigging method

C. Use the method from any similar-looking device

D. Participate only after equipment-specific instruction and authorized crew direction

### Explained answers and remediation

**O04-L1: Wait in the safe area and obtain the agreed clear instruction** Unclear communication requires resolution before movement. Cargo and passenger operations may use different signals. Reread O04 and explain the corrected action using the chapter practice.

**O04-L2: The landing area is obstructed** An obstructed landing area is an unresolved control. Schedule pressure and familiarity do not establish safe conditions. Reread O04 and explain the corrected action using the chapter practice.

**O04-L3: Participate only after equipment-specific instruction and authorized crew direction** Device-specific instruction and a controlled transfer remain necessary. Orientation does not qualify operators or riggers. Reread O04 and explain the corrected action using the chapter practice.

lessons.title: O05 — Arrival, living offshore and exposure at the worksite
lessons.body:
## O05 — Arrival, living offshore and exposure at the worksite

### Objectives

Complete a site-specific orientation; establish routes, contacts and restrictions; recognize dropped-object, hand, clothing and living-area hazards; respond to changing weather and extended duty.

Transport arrival and permission to begin work are separate events. Report to the designated person, confirm accountability and receive the facility-specific orientation before starting an assignment. Find out who is in charge, how the shift is organized, which areas are restricted, and what operations are occurring. Know the alarm meanings, muster arrangements, emergency contacts and alternate routes. Ask how a visitor obtains an escort or task authorization. A general course cannot provide the current layout or today's conflicting operations.

Walk the permitted route with the appropriate guide. Locate the actual muster area and understand an alternative if the normal path becomes unsafe. Identify where required protective equipment is worn and where equipment must be kept out of accommodation or food areas. Look for changes in floor level, open gratings, wet stairs, hoses and overhead work. Use handrails and maintain stable footing; do not carry a load that prevents seeing the route or using required support. Report damaged stairs, guards or lighting rather than normalizing them because other people pass that way.

Above and below are connected offshore work areas. A small tool dropped from height can strike someone far below, while a loose fitting may fall beyond a tidy-looking exclusion zone. Respect dropped-object controls and do not pass beneath overhead work. Workers assigned tools at height need the correct tool-retention system and training; tying an improvised cord to an unsuitable point can create another hazard. Report unsecured objects from a safe position. Do not reach over an edge to retrieve one or remove a barrier because the task appears paused.

Protect hands by understanding where movement can trap them. A door, hatch, pipe, transfer device or shifting cargo can close a gap suddenly. Use the designated handles and keep hands out of pinch points; a glove cannot prevent crushing. Select task-appropriate protection through the employer's assessment and instruction. Cut resistance, impact protection, chemical resistance and electrical protection are not interchangeable. Check condition, fit and compatibility. Fire-resistant clothing also has limits: damage, contamination, inappropriate layering or incorrect wearing can undermine protection. Follow the specified clothing requirements rather than treating a brand label as a complete protective system.

Living quarters are part of the work environment. Observe quiet periods, hygiene and smoking restrictions, keep escape routes clear, and store personal items where they cannot fall or obstruct movement. Report illness through the designated medical or supervisor process. Respect confidential personal information and maintain professional conduct in shared accommodation. Do not tolerate threats or harassment as an unavoidable feature of close quarters; use the reporting routes explained by the employer and seek immediate help for an urgent threat.

Weather can affect access, visibility, footing, vessel movement and evacuation options. Follow the facility's weather restrictions and announcements. Do not invent a personal wind or wave limit. If conditions change during a task, pause the affected work and notify the responsible supervisor. The same applies to fatigue from extended duty or interrupted rest. A revised schedule requires a revised readiness decision; a worker's presence offshore does not mean that person remains fit for every task.

### Worked situation

After arrival, a contractor is asked to carry equipment through a stairwell beneath scaffold work. The marked route is closed, and the alternative has not been explained. The contractor asks the site contact to identify an authorized route and coordinate the conflicting work. Choosing the closed route because it is shorter defeats both access control and dropped-object protection. Starting the task before orientation would also leave the worker uncertain about accountability and emergency routes.

### Practice and explained response

Explain why high-impact gloves do not justify placing a hand between moving cargo and a rail. The protection does not remove the crushing exposure. The safer response is to keep clear and use the authorized handling method, with the responsible crew controlling the movement.



### Learning checks

#### O05-L1

You reach the facility and are immediately asked to begin work before induction. What should happen?

A. Start because transport clearance covers the worksite

B. Obtain the site orientation and task authorization first

C. Learn the alarm meanings at the next drill

D. Ask a coworker to sign the induction record for you

#### O05-L2

A worker wearing impact gloves places a hand between shifting cargo and a rail. What is the main problem?

A. The glove color may be incorrect

B. The worker should add a second glove

C. The hand is still in a crushing zone

D. The task needs only a warning sign

#### O05-L3

A direct route passes under overhead maintenance. What is the safe decision?

A. Use an authorized alternative and respect the exclusion area

B. Walk quickly through the exclusion area

C. Wear a hard hat and ignore the barrier

D. Move the barrier when nobody is looking

### Explained answers and remediation

**O05-L1: Obtain the site orientation and task authorization first** Arrival does not establish site knowledge or work authorization. Resolve current routes, alarms, contacts and task controls first. Reread O05 and explain the corrected action using the chapter practice.

**O05-L2: The hand is still in a crushing zone** PPE cannot remove a crushing exposure. Keep the hand out and use the controlled handling method. Reread O05 and explain the corrected action using the chapter practice.

**O05-L3: Use an authorized alternative and respect the exclusion area** Dropped-object controls depend on separation. A hard hat and speed do not make an excluded route acceptable. Reread O05 and explain the corrected action using the chapter practice.

lessons.title: O06 — Applying SEMS to an ordinary work decision
lessons.body:
## O06 — Applying SEMS to an ordinary work decision

### Objectives

Explain how the safety and environmental management system affects a worker's job; distinguish stop-work and restart decisions; identify changes requiring review; communicate hazards and preserve accurate records.

An offshore safety and environmental management system connects management decisions to the conditions in which work occurs. For a worker, the practical question is not whether a binder exists. It is whether the correct information, people, procedure and protective arrangements are available for the actual task. On covered U.S. offshore operations, the operator's SEMS program includes documented arrangements for hazards, changes, procedures, training, equipment integrity, emergency response, learning from incidents and worker participation. Follow the program applicable to your facility and role.

Think of the system as a chain of decisions. Facility information describes what is present. Hazard analysis identifies how people or the environment could be harmed. A task-level job safety analysis makes those concerns concrete for the job. Operating procedures and safe work practices explain the authorized method. Training establishes who has the skills and knowledge to perform it. Equipment-integrity and pre-startup arrangements address whether the physical system is ready. A break in any link should not be covered up with another signature.

Before a task, participate in the briefing. State the step you will perform, the exposure you could encounter, the control you depend on and the person controlling the interface. Ask what happens if conditions change. If the work pack identifies one pump but the physical label identifies another, stop before intervention. A permit authorizes specified work under specified conditions; it does not make contradictory information harmless. Do not operate a valve to discover which equipment is connected.

Changes can be physical or organizational. A replacement component, revised procedure, different crew, temporary bypass or altered simultaneous operation can affect risk. Workers identify the change and refer it through the facility process; they do not decide that a change is “like for like” merely because a replacement fits. Management-of-change review and a task briefing serve related but different functions. Updating a JSA cannot by itself approve an engineering change, and an approved engineering change still needs communication to the people doing the work.

Stop-work authority means a person can raise a hazardous condition and initiate the site's safe stop process. Use a clear message about the location, exposure and requested hold. Do not create another emergency with an unplanned abrupt equipment action; follow the procedure for stopping safely. The facility also identifies ultimate work authority for operational safety decisions. Knowing that responsible role matters when a disagreement or unresolved hazard persists. The person who reports a concern is not automatically the person permitted to restart the equipment.

Employee participation includes contributing observations, asking questions and reporting unsafe conditions. Use the internal routes provided, and understand the available route for reporting concerns to BSEE for covered operations. A supervisor's reluctance to hear a concern does not erase that route. Use the current official reporting information provided in the source register or facility posting. Give factual information: what was observed, where, when and what exposure may remain. Do not alter evidence, speculate about motives or enter danger to collect proof.

Records should support the next decision. A truthful JSA, inspection report, handover or incident account identifies the actual condition and any remaining restriction. Do not sign for an inspection you did not perform, mark someone present when unaccounted for, or erase an unsuccessful observation to make a record look clean. Incident investigation and audits should lead to corrected conditions and verified learning. A completed form is not evidence that the physical control works.

### Worked situation

A valve replacement is delayed, so a supervisor proposes a temporary hose connection for one shift. A worker recognizes that the connection differs from the work pack and may affect pressure containment and routing. The worker requests a hold and refers the proposed change to the responsible engineering and operating authorities through the facility process. The worker does not select a hose rating or approve the bypass from this orientation. Restart follows the authorized review, suitable equipment, revised instructions and communication to affected crews.

### Practice and explained response

Who resolves a conflict between a schedule request and an unresolved control? Identify the facility's responsible authority and escalation route. A complete answer preserves the hold, communicates the specific hazard, and distinguishes authorization to resume from a general request to hurry.



### Learning checks

#### O06-L1

A temporary hose would change the planned equipment arrangement. Who should approve the change?

A. Any person who can attach the hose

B. The first worker to update the JSA

C. The delivery driver

D. The responsible authorities through the facility’s change process

#### O06-L2

After you initiate a safe stop for an unresolved hazard, what permits restart?

A. The time allocated for the task expires

B. The responsible authority confirms resolution and authorizes restart under the procedure

C. A coworker says the concern is probably minor

D. The person who reported it leaves the area

#### O06-L3

What is an accurate inspection record?

A. A signature based on someone else’s usual practice

B. A record with all unsuccessful observations removed

C. The actual observations, remaining restrictions and required action

D. A completed form without checking the equipment

### Explained answers and remediation

**O06-L1: The responsible authorities through the facility’s change process** A task worksheet does not approve an engineering or operational change. Refer the proposal through the applicable process. Reread O06 and explain the corrected action using the chapter practice.

**O06-L2: The responsible authority confirms resolution and authorizes restart under the procedure** The hold ends through the authorized restart decision after controls are resolved, not through time or reassurance. Reread O06 and explain the corrected action using the chapter practice.

**O06-L3: The actual observations, remaining restrictions and required action** Records must describe what occurred and what remains unresolved. A clean-looking form cannot substitute for an inspection. Reread O06 and explain the corrected action using the chapter practice.

lessons.title: O07 — Marine debris, spills and environmental accountability
lessons.body:
## O07 — Marine debris, spills and environmental accountability

### Objectives

Prevent loss of material to the sea; distinguish routine waste handling from release response; report a loss accurately; recognize that orientation does not replace required environmental training.

Marine debris begins as an ordinary work-planning problem: loose packaging, an unsecured lid, a damaged waste container or material staged where wind and movement can carry it away. Once in the water, an object may be difficult to recover and can harm wildlife, vessels or other users. Prevention is more reliable than trying to retrieve a lost item from an exposed edge.

Before unpacking or moving supplies, identify where wrapping, offcuts and small parts will go. Use the designated containers and secure them under the facility's arrangements. Keep lids or other closures effective; do not place light material on an open bin and assume it will remain there. Inspect the route and staging location for wind, drainage openings, edges and nearby work. A tidy indoor packing method may fail on an exposed deck. Ask the responsible person to correct a damaged container or unsuitable staging arrangement before material is released.

Keep waste streams identified and separated according to the site plan. A food container, contaminated absorbent, oily rag, chemical container and damaged battery do not become the same waste because they fit in one bag. Consult the label, applicable product information and designated environmental contact when classification is uncertain. Do not pour unwanted liquid into a drain or overboard. Do not use an unlabeled container to make a material easier to transport. The person responsible for waste handling determines the authorized storage and disposal route.

Report a dropped object or release promptly. From a safe position, identify the material if known, approximate amount, location, time, movement and any immediate exposure. State uncertainty instead of inventing a quantity. Keep others out of the affected area and follow the site's notification instructions. Do not climb outside rails, lean overboard or enter the water to recover property. Recovery decisions belong to authorized personnel using a planned method.

A spill may involve more than pollution. Vapors, fire, slippery footing, toxicity or pressure can make an apparently small release dangerous. Do not judge an unknown material only by the size of the puddle. Follow the alarm, isolation and withdrawal arrangements for your role. An incidental cleanup is appropriate only when the employer's procedure, training, equipment and conditions establish that it is within your assigned capability. If those facts are missing, obtain the appropriate response. Never wash a spill away to improve appearances or conceal the event.

Marine-debris instruction has its own applicable program requirements. BSEE's offshore marine-debris program calls for recurring worker training and operator training records. This orientation explains prevention decisions but does not silently certify completion of every required annual program or operator-specific module. Verify the separate requirement with the employer, record the actual training completed and use the current official guidance. The same distinction applies to emergency spill response and hazardous-waste duties.

### Worked situation

A crew opens a pallet of parts on a windy deck. Plastic wrap begins moving toward the edge. A worker suggests stepping outside the rail to catch it. The useful intervention is to stop unpacking, alert the crew, secure remaining material and arrange proper waste containment. If material has already entered the sea, report it accurately. Creating a fall or person-overboard event to avoid reporting debris would compound the incident.

### Practice and explained response

A drip tray contains an unidentified liquid and is close to overflowing. What should you report? State the location, observed condition, unknown identity and any immediate exposure. Keep clear and obtain the responsible response. Do not identify it by smell, mix it with another waste or choose a cleanup method from appearance alone.



### Learning checks

#### O07-L1

Plastic wrap is blowing toward the deck edge. What is the best immediate response?

A. Stop unpacking, secure remaining material and alert the crew from safety

B. Climb outside the rail to catch it

C. Wash it toward a drain

D. Continue and report only if someone complains

#### O07-L2

A tray contains an unidentified liquid. What should you do?

A. Smell it closely to identify it

B. Pour it into the nearest waste drum

C. Assume it is water because it is clear

D. Report the unknown material and obtain the authorized response

#### O07-L3

Does completing this orientation automatically satisfy every marine-debris training requirement?

A. Yes, for all future years

B. No; confirm the applicable recurring and operator-specific training separately

C. Only if the learner signs twice

D. Yes, if no debris incident has occurred

### Explained answers and remediation

**O07-L1: Stop unpacking, secure remaining material and alert the crew from safety** Prevent further loss without exposing a person to a fall. Report any loss and let authorized personnel decide recovery. Reread O07 and explain the corrected action using the chapter practice.

**O07-L2: Report the unknown material and obtain the authorized response** Unknown identity means the hazards and disposal route are unresolved. Appearance is not a safe classification method. Reread O07 and explain the corrected action using the chapter practice.

**O07-L3: No; confirm the applicable recurring and operator-specific training separately** The orientation does not replace a separate required recurring program or its actual training records. Reread O07 and explain the corrected action using the chapter practice.

lessons.title: O08 — Offshore alarms, muster, evacuation and recovery
lessons.body:
## O08 — Offshore alarms, muster, evacuation and recovery

### Objectives

Act on the facility's alarm and muster instructions; preserve accountability; identify the limits of orientation during abandonment or rescue; distinguish emergency reentry from authorization to resume work.

An offshore emergency can affect escape routes and transport options at the same time. Preparation therefore depends on the actual facility plan: alarm meanings, reporting method, primary and alternate muster locations, assigned emergency roles and available evacuation arrangements. Learn these on arrival, not while an alarm is sounding. Confirm how you will receive instructions in noisy work areas or accommodation, and tell the site contact if you cannot perceive the alarm or understand the briefing.

When an alarm or instruction requires withdrawal, follow the site procedure for making your immediate activity safe only within your assigned role and without delaying escape. Do not remain to diagnose the alarm, finish a short task or retrieve personal property. Move by the instructed safe route. If that route is blocked or exposed, use the site's alternative arrangement and communicate your location from safety. Do not enter smoke, an unknown atmosphere or a restricted area because it appears to provide a shortcut.

At muster, report to the accountability person and remain available for instructions. Identify yourself and provide factual information about anyone you last saw, including location and time if known. Do not mark another worker present based on an assumption, leave without being recorded, or circulate rumors that complicate the count. If you are assigned a muster role, follow the specific training for that role. Being helpful does not authorize an untrained person to conduct a search.

Evacuation and abandonment are controlled operations. Lifeboats, rafts, transfer equipment and passenger positions have equipment-specific procedures. Follow the designated crew and your required survival training. This course does not provide a universal water-entry method or authorize a practice jump. Water entry can introduce impact, cold, entanglement, burning-surface or separation hazards; never use it as an improvised shortcut. Raise a concern if you cannot use the planned arrangement and obtain the responsible instruction before an emergency where practicable.

If someone goes overboard, raise the alarm immediately using the vessel or facility's method, report the location and maintain observation from safety if you can. Do not enter the water or improvise a rescue from an unprotected edge. Trained responders and the responsible marine crew coordinate recovery. If assisting from a protected location, perform only the actions you are trained and directed to perform. A second casualty makes the original recovery harder.

Medical response offshore also depends on communication. Give the precise facility location, access route, observed condition and known hazards. Follow the trained responder's instructions within your competence. Do not enter an unsafe scene, move an injured person casually, or provide treatment for which you are not trained. Emergency transport decisions involve medical and operational authorities, weather and suitable transport. Your factual report helps those people plan; a general safety credential does not transfer their authority to you.

After an all-clear, confirm what it permits. Return to accommodation, reentry to a deck and restart of a maintenance task may be separate decisions. Permits, isolations, damaged equipment and conflicting work may need reassessment. Report any control disturbed during the emergency. Participate in the debrief with observations about routes, communications and accountability; record deficiencies so they can be corrected before the next event.

### Worked situation

During an alarm, a worker reaches the primary route and sees smoke beyond the next door. The worker withdraws from that exposure, uses the briefed alternate route and reports to the designated accountability contact. At muster, the worker reports where a colleague was last seen but does not mark that colleague safe. After the all-clear, the worker obtains the responsible task restart instructions instead of assuming the earlier permit automatically remains valid.

### Practice and explained response

Why is “I will go back and check” an unsafe default when someone is missing? The missing person creates a response need, but not safe entry conditions or rescue competence. Give the last-known location to the response team, remain accounted for and perform only an assigned, trained action from safety.


### Learning checks

#### O08-L1

The primary evacuation route is exposed to smoke. What should you do?

A. Run through before the smoke gets thicker

B. Return to retrieve belongings

C. Use the briefed safe alternative and communicate your location

D. Follow an unmarked shortcut into a process area

#### O08-L2

A colleague is missing at muster. What information is useful?

A. The factual last-known location and time, without marking the person safe

B. An assumption that the colleague took another boat

C. A promise to search alone

D. A report that everyone is present to avoid delay

#### O08-L3

An all-clear allows return to the accommodation. Can maintenance automatically restart?

A. Yes, all permits are renewed by an all-clear

B. Yes, if the supervisor is busy

C. Yes, if no tools were moved

D. No; obtain the task-specific restart decision and reassess disturbed controls

### Explained answers and remediation

**O08-L1: Use the briefed safe alternative and communicate your location** Do not enter an unsafe route. Use the site’s alternative arrangement and preserve accountability. Reread O08 and explain the corrected action using the chapter practice.

**O08-L2: The factual last-known location and time, without marking the person safe** Accurate last-known information supports trained responders. Do not invent accountability or create an untrained rescue. Reread O08 and explain the corrected action using the chapter practice.

**O08-L3: No; obtain the task-specific restart decision and reassess disturbed controls** Emergency reentry and task restart are separate decisions. Permits and controls may need review. Reread O08 and explain the corrected action using the chapter practice.

Mark Pass, Needs practice, or Not assessed, with observed evidence. A critical error stops the scenario. Explain the reason, reteach, and administer the changed retry. Every criterion must pass; do not average away an unsafe intervention. These stations assess orientation decisions, not equipment operating skills.

lessons.title: 1. Arrival during a changing operation
lessons.body:
## 1. Arrival during a changing operation

**Materials:** fictional arrival card: “You are delivering a sealed parts box. Rig-up is underway. The usual stairs are inside a lifting boundary. Your escort has not arrived. The gate contact can reach the area controller.” Draw a safe waiting point at the gate and mark the ordinary stairs closed.

**Task:** Describe and role-play your check-in and movement decision. **Criteria:** identifies delivery purpose; remains at safe waiting point; confirms area controller/escort; does not assume experience grants access; requests the current route and emergency/accountability briefing; recognizes the rig-up phase changes access.

**Critical error:** crossing the lifting boundary or climbing an improvised route. **Worked resolution:** check in, wait for coordinated access and escort as required, learn the current emergency instructions, then use only the approved route. **Retry:** rig is operating but a maintenance crew has temporarily removed a walkway guard. The learner must recognize the changed route rather than treating the operating phase alone as clearance.

lessons.title: 2. Pipe movement and pressure boundary
lessons.body:
## 2. Pipe movement and pressure boundary

**Materials:** draw rack A, handling path B, fixed wall C, and safe pedestrian path D. A tubular is suspended over B. A hose at C is labelled “pressure status not verified.” A radio card states “communication with operator lost.”

**Task:** Select a safe position, explain the hold, and communicate concerns. **Criteria:** avoids B and the pinch position between load and C; does not grab the tubular; uses the agreed stop/hold process; identifies lost communications; does not touch or tighten the hose; seeks responsible verification rather than assuming a silent pump means safe.

**Critical errors:** entering under the load, hands-on intervention with moving pipe, or manipulating the unverified line. **Worked resolution:** remain on D outside boundaries, notify the controlling personnel, hold affected operations, and let authorized people restore controls. **Retry:** movement has stopped but the load remains suspended. The learner still respects the exposure and does not enter merely because it is stationary.

lessons.title: 3. Land hazards after weather changes
lessons.body:
## 3. Land hazards after weather changes

**Materials:** trench card: “Inspected before dawn. Heavy rain since then. Water visible. The crew wants a short entry.” Pond card: “Lined produced-water pond; barrier moved; tool at the bottom; depth unknown.”

**Task:** Explain the decisions and notifications for both locations. **Criteria:** holds trench entry for competent-person reassessment and required controls; recognizes water and changed soil conditions; does not select shoring independently; stays outside pond barrier; recognizes slipping/drowning/chemical/atmosphere concerns; activates trained response rather than entering if a person falls.

**Critical errors:** approving a quick unprotected entry or entering the pond for retrieval/rescue. **Worked resolution:** restore control through the responsible site personnel and preserve safe exclusion; duration and apparent depth do not remove the hazards. **Retry:** no rain, but heavy equipment has moved next to the trench and cracks are observed. The learner recognizes a new reassessment trigger.

lessons.title: 4. Offshore transfer and accountability
lessons.body:
## 4. Offshore transfer and accountability

**Materials:** manifest card with the learner's name missing; transfer card: “Crew has not given boarding permission; vessel motion is increasing”; site card listing two muster points and a controller-selected safe point B. These are classroom cards, not a real transport instruction.

**Task:** Resolve travel readiness, state boarding limits, and make a simulated arrival check-in. **Criteria:** corrects manifest through the responsible dispatcher; waits for authorized crew instruction; reports unclear briefing or unready equipment; does not jump or improvise transfer; checks in on arrival; identifies current emergency instructions and safe point B.

**Critical errors:** boarding without clearance, inventing a transfer technique, or bypassing the manifest. **Worked resolution:** hold until records, equipment, and crew-controlled conditions are ready; follow site-specific induction after arrival. **Retry:** manifest correct but the assigned flotation equipment is damaged. The learner holds for approved replacement and instruction rather than accepting the corrected paperwork as complete readiness.

lessons.title: 5. Integrated handover, exposure, and restart
lessons.body:
## 5. Integrated handover, exposure, and restart

**Materials:** handover card: “A dust-control enclosure was removed; one machine is isolated with a guard off; gas all-clear issued for the area; lifting permit remains suspended; visitor not yet checked out.”

**Task:** Give a structured incoming-shift handover and identify what may resume. **Criteria:** reports each unresolved condition; preserves isolation; does not substitute PPE for the removed enclosure; distinguishes area all-clear from lift authorization; resolves visitor accountability; identifies responsible corrective action owners; records unknowns rather than inventing safe status.

**Critical errors:** authorizing machine startup, lift restart, or uncontrolled exposure solely because of the all-clear. **Worked resolution:** transfer the actual limits and require each task's controls and authority to be restored independently. **Retry:** all equipment is restored but the incoming crew has not been briefed on a relocated emergency route. The learner completes communication before dependent work.

## References

- [IADC program page](https://iadc.org/accreditation/rigpass/): current public program description; establishes orientation scope and the separate accreditation process.
- [IADC public subject benchmark](https://iadc.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/SCO-02-Curriculum_Rev0.pdf): SCO-02 Revision 0, 30 October 2020. Used to check subject breadth, not copied as instruction or represented as the latest private accreditation standard.
- [IADC program handbook](https://iadc.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/SCO-01_AccreditationProcedures_2nd-edition_rev2.pdf): second edition, revision 2, 15 March 2021. Accreditation and delivery rules apply to approved providers; VNDRLY does not claim that status.
- [OSHA drilling overview](https://www.osha.gov/etools/oil-and-gas/drilling): operating phases and task-specific assessment.
- [OSHA drilling ahead](https://www.osha.gov/etools/oil-and-gas/drilling/drilling-ahead): tubular movement and rig-floor exposure.
- [OSHA rigging up](https://www.osha.gov/etools/oil-and-gas/drilling/rigging-up): changing equipment, access and assembly conditions.

- [OSHA extraction hazards](https://www.osha.gov/oil-and-gas-extraction/hazards): pressure, machinery, transport and exposure context.

- [OSHA excavation technical guidance](https://www.osha.gov/otm/section-5-construction-operations/chapter-2): water and changed-condition inspection concerns.
- [IOGP human performance](https://www.iogp.org/workstreams/safety/safety/human-performance/): organizational support for reliable decisions; VNDRLY examples are original.
- [FBI emergency safety guidance](https://www.fbi.gov/how-we-can-help-you/active-shooter-safety-resources/active-shooter-event-quick-reference-guide): avoid threat, seek safety, notify and follow responders; no tactical intervention training is supplied.

lessons.title: SEMS teaching reference — what the elements mean at the worker interface
lessons.body:
## SEMS teaching reference — what the elements mean at the worker interface

Use this reference with O06. It explains connections, not a substitute operator SEMS manual.

| Element | What the worker should recognize and do |
|---|---|
| General management arrangements | Know the assigned responsibility and escalation line. A procedure cannot work if nobody has the authority or resources to implement it; report that gap rather than inventing authority. |
| Safety and environmental information | Use current equipment identity and hazard information. If the field label and work pack disagree, hold the affected activity and have the responsible people resolve the discrepancy. |
| Hazard analysis | Identify the exposure path and affected people. Contribute what you see at the worksite; a facility assessment does not excuse skipping the actual task briefing. |
| Management of change | Report a departure from the approved arrangement before using it. A temporary workaround can alter risk just as a permanent modification can. |
| Operating procedures | Obtain the current authorized method and understand its limits. Stop for an unexplained step rather than combining fragments of different revisions. |
| Safe work practices | Apply the relevant permit and protection arrangements. A signed permit must correspond to the actual task and conditions; it is not blanket authorization. |
| Training | Perform only the assigned duties for which you have the necessary instruction and competence. Report an unfamiliar operation before someone mistakes your presence for qualification. |
| Mechanical integrity | Report leaks, damage and degraded controls. Do not bypass a protective device to maintain production or sign a check you did not perform. |
| Pre-startup review | Recognize that completion of installation or maintenance is not the same as authorization to start. The responsible review must resolve readiness and communicate restrictions. |
| Emergency response | Know your alarm, route, muster and reporting actions. Leave specialist response to people trained and assigned to perform it. |
| Incident investigation | Supply accurate observations and preserve evidence from safety. Distinguish what you saw from what you heard, and do not hide near misses. |
| Audits | Cooperate with truthful records and descriptions of actual practice. An audit is an opportunity to identify gaps, not to stage controls that disappear afterward. |
| Records and documentation | Identify the task, version, actual response and remaining action. Keep records through the employer's prescribed process; do not invent retention periods or destroy unsuccessful attempts. |
| Stop-work authority | Raise a specific hazardous condition and initiate the safe hold procedure. Seek resolution without creating an uncontrolled equipment action. |
| Ultimate work authority | Know which designated role makes final operational safety decisions on the facility. Escalate unresolved conflicts through that route; seniority alone is not a substitute for designation. |
| Employee participation | Contribute to briefings, improvement discussions and hazard reporting. Ask whether the proposed control works in the real work arrangement. |
| Reporting unsafe conditions | Use the site's reporting process and understand the available BSEE reporting route for covered operations. Report factual concerns without exposing yourself to gather proof. |

lessons.title: Drilling Well Control — program and instructor guide
lessons.body:
# Drilling Well Control — program and instructor guide

VUC005 · VNDRLY-owned program · Material package version 1.0

lessons.title: Audience and purpose
lessons.body:
## Audience and purpose

The program serves drilling personnel at awareness, introductory, driller, and supervisor responsibilities. Its purpose is to teach pressure reasoning, influx prevention and recognition, approved response, circulation planning, equipment limitations, and team decision making. Completion must be recorded at the assessed pathway and equipment configuration. A surface knowledge result must not be represented as subsea operating competence.

This is not an IADC-accredited WellSharp course and does not award an IADC card. Employer authorization, required external qualifications, equipment-specific training, and applicable legal requirements remain separate. The course must not be advertised as an externally recognized equivalent without the necessary independent approval.

lessons.title: Prerequisites and placement
lessons.body:
## Prerequisites and placement

All learners need the language and numeracy support necessary to interpret warnings and communicate accurately. Awareness learners need basic drilling-site orientation. Introductory learners need calculator use, decimal arithmetic, unit conversion, and an understanding of a well schematic. Driller candidates require role experience or a documented preparatory pathway, familiarity with the actual console/procedure being assessed, and the introductory knowledge. Supervisor candidates require the driller knowledge and demonstrated ability to review a well program, calculation sheet, equipment limitations, and contingencies. An instructor records placement rather than assuming job title proves readiness.

Before instruction, ask learners to distinguish measured and vertical depth, compute 10% of a volume, read a pressure trend, and explain the difference between a measurement and a limit. Errors guide preparatory teaching; they are not grounds for humiliating a learner or skipping the prerequisite.

lessons.title: Delivery and learning objectives
lessons.body:
## Delivery and learning objectives

Teach the eighteen chapters in order. Each contains an explanation, a worked case, common errors or decision traps, and practice with an explained answer. Use the separate formative checks after each chapter. Teach-back is required: the learner explains the reasoning, not only the chosen answer. In calculation work, insist on units, datum, assumptions, and a reasonableness check.

| Chapter | Observable outcome | Application |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Distinguish pressure contributions and use TVD | Pressure sketch and calculation |
| 2 | Calculate layered support, density change and ECD; state limitations | Independent calculation review |
| 3 | Reconcile volume and identify unsafe trip discrepancies | Trip-tank exercise |
| 4 | Identify and communicate credible influx evidence | Detection simulation |
| 5 | Trace barriers and verify equipment suitability | Barrier and test-record review |
| 6 | Apply configured response and preserve uncertain observations | Response simulation and log |
| 7 | Calculate and challenge a simplified circulation schedule | Planning worksheet and simulation |
| 8 | Explain gas/formation limits and reject unsupported interventions | Constrained-decision case |
| 9 | Identify subsea and MPD interface changes | Equipment-specific extension |
| 10 | Resolve readiness, lead handover and defend restart restrictions | Supervisor case conference |
| 11 | Check multi-step calculations, fluid placement and uncertainty | Independent worksheet review |
| 12 | Distinguish competing explanations and preserve controlled response | Fault-injection simulation |
| 13 | Recognize off-bottom/noncirculating model limits and specialist-method boundaries | Supervisor decision review |
| 14 | Communicate, protect personnel, and debrief with measurable improvement | All practical stations |
| 15 | Interpret formation/fluid ambiguity and protect against trapped pressure | Station H |
| 16 | Verify monitoring, alarms and control indications | Station G |
| 17 | Explain separator limits and configured emergency functions | Stations D/E |
| 18 | Control transitions, combine margins and verify completion | Stations D/F |

Awareness learners study all chapter narratives with instructor support, but receive no operational endorsement from them. Introductory learners complete the calculations and tabletop cases. Driller and supervisor pathways additionally require the configured simulator evaluations. Chapter 9's theoretical coverage does not replace a subsea practical endorsement.

lessons.title: Instructor preparation
lessons.body:
## Instructor preparation

Use a competent well-control instructor for operational pathways. Before each delivery, the instructor checks numerical examples independently, reviews source currency and applicability, and verifies that simulator instructions match its configuration. For console assessment, attach the simulator manufacturer's approved operating procedure and case configuration to the assessment record. This is necessary equipment input, not an invitation to substitute a generic valve sequence from memory.

All practical activity takes place in a classroom or simulator with no connection to live well controls. Clearly label training cases. No pressure-bearing field experiment, gas release, intentional influx, or live emergency exercise is authorized by these materials.

Allow sufficient time for remediation; completion is based on demonstrated outcomes rather than attendance alone. Allocate substantial supervised practice for operational pathways. Record actual instruction and simulation time separately. No claim is made that the schedule satisfies another organization's accreditation hours.

lessons.title: Evaluation rules
lessons.body:
## Evaluation rules

Formative checks are open-book learning activities with explanations. Incorrect responses require the named chapter review and a new explanation in the learner's own words. Final assessment is separate and controlled; the instructor key must not be distributed in the learner packet.

The full controlled final contains 72 single-best-answer questions, one point each; at least 58 correct is required for the knowledge pass. The awareness form has 26 conceptual questions spanning all eighteen domains and requires 21 correct. Use the protected key and record domain results. Calculators and the supplied formula reference are allowed; coaching and the answer key are not. Accessibility arrangements may change presentation or time without supplying answers or omitting objectives. The final assessment and pathway-specific practical score sheets must be complete before issuing a program credential. Knowledge and practical results are distinct. No partial classroom attendance or successful quiz may be relabelled as operational competence. A learner who has completed only knowledge receives a transcript stating that fact, not a driller or supervisor practical endorsement.

| Pathway | Instruction and learning checks | Final | Required demonstration |
|---|---|---|---|
| Awareness | All narratives; calculation reasoning discussed with instructor; conceptual teach-back | Awareness 26-item form, 21 correct | Station B in reporting role; no console operation |
| Introductory | All chapters, exercises and 36 formative checks remediated | Full 72-item form, 58 correct | Station A calculation and B recognition; C tabletop log |
| Driller | All chapters and checks, configured equipment/procedure familiarization | Full form, 58 correct | A–D, G and H; E for any subsea/MPD scope claimed |
| Supervisor | All chapters and checks, planning and leadership practice | Full form, 58 correct, plus protected written case at least 16/20 with no critical failure | A–D and F–H; E for any subsea/MPD scope claimed |

The full program's operational scope is conventional drilling well-control reasoning and assessed response on the recorded simulator configuration. Chapter 13 teaches recognition and decision boundaries for specialist noncirculating methods; it does not award a stripping, snubbing, bullheading, or live specialist-method qualification. Record that restriction rather than implying mastery from awareness instruction.

Critical practical errors include ignoring credible influx evidence, operating outside the supplied procedure, inventing safety-critical data, continuing beyond a stated limit, concealing a failed barrier, or authorizing restart with an unresolved critical restriction. Stop the exercise safely, record the observed action, teach the gap, and reassess with a different case. Do not average a critical failure away with arithmetic points.

After a failed final assessment, give domain-level feedback without disclosing the controlled key. Require targeted instruction before another attempt. After three failed attempts, require a documented retraining plan and instructor review before a new assessment. These are VNDRLY course rules, not claims about IADC policy.

lessons.title: Credential and refresher policy
lessons.body:
## Credential and refresher policy

Record learner identity, program version, pathway, knowledge score, practical result, simulator/equipment scope, assessor identity, assessment date, and any restrictions. The credential must state VNDRLY/U and the actual assessed scope. It does not independently authorize live well operations.

Require refresher instruction and reassessment after a significant role/equipment/procedure change, an identified competence gap, prolonged absence assessed by the employer, or an incident exposing a training need. Applicable external renewal requirements must still be met. Do not invent a universal legal expiry. The employer's competence system determines ongoing deployment authorization.

lessons.title: Records and quality review
lessons.body:
## Records and quality review

Keep the learner's calculation sheets, case observations, signed score sheets, remediation record, and final result. Record what was actually demonstrated. A completed blank form is not evidence of an assessment. Review learner errors for teaching defects: repeated datum errors may indicate an unclear diagram; repeated procedure failures may indicate inadequate configuration familiarization. Correct instructional defects before the next delivery, preserving the version used for existing results.


---
