lessons.title: VUC037 delivery guide and practical assessment packet
lessons.body: # VUC037 delivery guide and practical assessment packet

lessons.title: Delivery, resources and completion
lessons.body:
## Delivery, resources and completion

Audience and prerequisite check: confirm basic industrial safety, technical drawing literacy, algebra and unit conversion. Give the learner a diagnostic task converting 0.250 in to 6.35 mm and identifying the difference between a measured thickness and a nominal thickness. Incorrect answers require coached preparation before the numerical workshops. No actual tank entry, radiation work, live hot tapping or pressure testing is authorized by this course.

Plan 64 instructional hours: 12 teaching and discussion; 12 worked application; 8 supplied-criteria decision laboratories (C37-1 through C37-4, including changed cases); 8 examination/qualification-record review; 16 practical stations; 4 coached remediation; 4 final assessment and feedback. This is a planned delivery allocation, not an assertion that a learner has attended. Adjust support time to demonstrated need without deleting objectives. The 16-hour practical block requires small groups and individual observation; do not let one learner's group demonstration stand for everyone. Controlled-standard lookup activities are optional extensions to this available-source delivery, not a claim of independently verified code-application competence.

Provide authorized current references from the source register, calculator, coursebook, technical workshops, printed forms, scaled tank/weld/plate drawings and the synthetic records below. For actual instrument and survey tasks provide a suitable UT instrument, probes/couplant, traceable reference blocks, known-thickness specimens with controlled defects, an instructor-approved written procedure, a level/survey instrument or suitable training rig, stable benchmark targets, rules/tape, safe coating-thickness instruments and coated panels. Use only nonhazardous clean training specimens and isolated equipment. The assessor verifies equipment suitability and reference values before each session. Do not substitute a screenshot for the learner's hands-on measurement at P05 or P11.

The instructor must be competent in the tank-inspection subject and the examinations they supervise. Specialized method or engineering demonstrations need the appropriate qualified person. This guide does not confer those qualifications. Before delivery, the instructor checks current adopted editions, local rules and equipment procedures, resolving changes in the packet rather than teaching superseded limits.

For every station score five criteria 0–2: 2 correct and independently demonstrated; 1 safe but incomplete or requiring prompting; 0 absent, wrong or unsafe. Pass at least 8/10, with every starred critical criterion scored 2. Stop unsafe demonstrations immediately; do not create a real hazardous condition to test the response. Preserve the result, teach the missed reasoning, then use the changed case. Two unsuccessful reassessments require an individualized instruction plan and a fresh equivalent task before further assessment.

The VNDRLY learning credential under the available-source basis requires: all 24 lessons and 48 formative checks corrected with reasoning; all eight workshops, eight advanced labs and twenty mechanism/repair cases completed using their supplied records; all four supplementary C37 decision laboratories passed; the supplementary bottom-qualification case passed; all 24 stations passed; and the separately proctored final passed. It is a storage-tank inspection learning credential, not API 653 certification, employer appointment, professional license or qualification to perform every NDE method. Where required hands-on tasks remain outstanding, record incomplete. Record optional controlled-standard extension results separately; do not infer those competencies from this course completion. Issue the credential with the program version and available-source scope visible.

Set a three-year VNDRLY learning review, or earlier following a material change in standards, role, technology, service or demonstrated knowledge deficiency. This is a program maintenance choice; it does not claim to replace an external certification's renewal rules. Refresher work addresses changed requirements and demonstrated gaps, with reassessment of affected tasks. Preserve original completion/version records.

lessons.title: Common recording form
lessons.body:
## Common recording form

Learner____ Program/version____ Date____ Assessor/competence____ Station____

Equipment/procedure/reference edition____ Supplied record ID____ Actual observations/raw readings____

Criterion scores 1__/2 2__/2 3__/2 4__/2 5__/2 Total__/10 Critical error/details____

Result: pass / incomplete / reassessment required. Missing evidence____ Remediation____

Changed task issued____ Reassessment date/result____ Learner acknowledgment____ Assessor signature____

Retain raw drawings, calculations, readings and original attempts with this form. Record simulations as simulations. No fabricated tank release, attendance, field performance or learner credential is part of authoring this packet.

lessons.title: P01 — Asset identity and authority
lessons.body:
## P01 — Asset identity and authority

Give the learner Q01's T-37/T-73 records and a blank identity sheet. Require a source-by-source reconciliation and a held-decision list. Observe: (1) separates tags; (2) distinguishes dimensions from material identity; (3)* excludes untraceable evidence; (4) identifies responsible engineering/owner decisions; (5) records useful independent inspection work. Changed task: material certificate valid but diameter disagreement remains. Do not credit copying the original answer without identifying which uncertainty changed.

lessons.title: P02 — Service-change screening
lessons.body:
## P02 — Service-change screening

Supply an old envelope of 28 ft at SG 0.75 and proposed SG 0.90. Learner calculates demand ratio and equal-head comparison, then drafts a review request. Criteria: (1) ratio 1.20; (2) comparison 23.333 ft; (3)* does not authorize that level; (4) includes vent/roof/foundation/material compatibility concerns; (5) names updated operating controls and verification. Changed task: density unchanged but pumping rate increases; learner must shift attention to the changed flow/protection basis.

lessons.title: P03 — Inspection map and limitations
lessons.body:
## P03 — Inspection map and limitations

Use D03's plate coverage and a blank 120-plate grid. Learner marks full, partial and inaccessible plates and writes a conclusion. Criteria: (1) all categories recorded; (2) no invented area percentage; (3)* no whole-bottom acceptance from partial evidence; (4) confirmation/method capability identified; (5) targeted next examination plan. Changed task: one formerly accessible plate becomes obstructed; assess whether the learner updates actual rather than planned coverage.

lessons.title: P04 — Access stop decision
lessons.body:
## P04 — Access stop decision

Use a tabletop permit scenario only: isolation unverified, atmosphere record stale, proposed entry to finish readings. Criteria: (1) recognizes unresolved boundary; (2)* declines entry; (3) identifies permit/isolation/monitoring roles; (4)* avoids unprotected rescue entry in the injected collapse scenario; (5) states restart evidence. Changed task: permitted entry loses ventilation. No physical hazardous entry is performed.

lessons.title: P05 — Actual thickness measurement
lessons.body:
## P05 — Actual thickness measurement

Use the verified UT instrument, written procedure, reference blocks and instructor-measured specimens. The assessor records specimen truth values and permitted measurement tolerance before giving the specimens to the learner; seal that sheet until scoring. Learner configures, verifies, measures at marked points, repeats and performs the required final check. Criteria: (1) appropriate probe/material/range selection; (2)* correct calibration and verification under procedure; (3) repeatable mapped readings within the pre-established tolerance; (4) recognizes uncertain signals rather than selecting a favorable display; (5)* responds to an injected failed final check by identifying affected data. Changed task: different known thickness/material or coating arrangement requiring the appropriate setup. If equipment is unavailable, mark this station incomplete; a calculation is not a substitute.

lessons.title: P06 — Rate and interval interpretation
lessons.body:
## P06 — Rate and interval interpretation

Supply 8.0 mm at year 0, 7.6 at year 4, 7.0 at year 6, required 5.8. Criteria: (1) long rate 0.1667; (2) recent 0.30; (3) projected life 4 years at recent rate; (4)* no automatic 4 year inspection interval; (5) investigates acceleration/uncertainty and records assumptions. Changed task: current 6.4, recent rate 0.60, life 1 year. Require the learner to revise all affected conclusions.

lessons.title: P07 — Local fill-height calculation
lessons.body:
## P07 — Local fill-height calculation

Supply S = 20,000 psi, E = 0.85, t = 0.220 in, D = 70 ft, G = 1.0 and the localized equation. Proposed head 21 ft. Criteria: (1) correct units; (2) numerator 3740; (3) H = 20.5495 ft; (4)* rejects 21 ft under supplied relation; (5) states other-load and whole-tank limits. Changed task: G = 0.85 gives 24.1758 ft; learner must not turn this numerical change into an unrestricted service approval.

lessons.title: P08 — Local area and pit map
lessons.body:
## P08 — Local area and pit map

Use D01 and D02. Learner draws profiles and pit lines, calculates criteria and marks controlling conditions. Criteria: (1) correct L and controlling profile; (2) future loss included once; (3) pit aggregate measured by the stated line; (4)* failing average/minimum/aggregate not hidden; (5) correct actual reference applicability recorded. Changed task: D01's thinner third reading; require reconsideration of sampling length, not only a new average.

lessons.title: P09 — Bottom projection
lessons.body:
## P09 — Bottom projection

Supply starting minimum 0.230 in, rates 0.004/0.008 in/year, proposed 9 years, minimum 0.100 in. Criteria: (1) total rate 0.012; (2) future 0.122 in; (3) mathematical limit 10.8333 years; (4)* no acceptance of unexamined regions; (5) separates annular/critical-zone and interval requirements. Changed task: underside rate 0.012, total 0.016, future 0.086; learner rejects 9 years.

lessons.title: P10 — Junction and leak record
lessons.body:
## P10 — Junction and leak record

Give a scaled sketch with shell, annular plate, remote bottom, damp external edge and adjacent rainwater drain. Supply annular criterion.180 in and reading.165. Criteria: (1) identifies location-specific criterion; (2) fails thickness; (3) distinguishes possible leak sources; (4)* proposes no intrusive live probing; (5) preserves weld/settlement evidence and disposition. Changed task: thickness repaired but examination missing; release remains pending.

lessons.title: P11 — Actual survey and interpretation
lessons.body:
## P11 — Actual survey and interpretation

Use a safe eight-target training rig, stable benchmark and suitable verified instrument. Before delivery, the assessor independently establishes target elevations, records tolerance from the instrument/procedure and sets one local departure among the targets. Learner checks datum, takes and records all readings, closes/checks the survey and plots the profile. Criteria: (1)* verifies datum and instrument; (2) maps actual points; (3) readings within pre-established tolerance; (4) identifies local departure without declaring an unsupported acceptance limit; (5) records conditions/limitations. Changed task: move the benchmark or omit a target in the supplied second record; require recognition and resurvey/coverage action. A prerecorded plot alone cannot earn the hands-on portion.

lessons.title: P12 — Roof system assessment
lessons.body:
## P12 — Roof system assessment

Use photographs or a clean mockup showing a blocked drain, low-side roof position and a documented compartment leak. Criteria: (1) recognizes drainage and buoyancy issues; (2) evaluates supports/seals/obstructions as relevant; (3)* restricts unverified access; (4) proposes controlled recovery/inspection; (5) retains leak finding after roof levels. Changed task: clear drain but damaged support-leg record; learner must not call the system restored.

lessons.title: P13 — Safeguard functional evidence
lessons.body:
## P13 — Safeguard functional evidence

Use a vent record marked cleaned/not tested and a trip record with output bypass active. Criteria: (1) distinguishes cleaning/testing; (2) identifies active bypass; (3)* does not credit unavailable protection; (4) specifies as-found/as-left and restoration evidence; (5) assigns responsible operating decision. Changed task: two alarms share frozen transmitter; learner identifies common dependency.

lessons.title: P14 — CP record review
lessons.body:
## P14 — CP record review

Provide D14: criterion requires designated instant-off points; record contains only an on-reading at perimeter; electrode check absent. Criteria: (1) identifies state mismatch; (2) location mismatch; (3)* withholds unsupported protection conclusion; (4) requires valid electrode/method records; (5) refers adjustment/design to competent corrosion personnel. Changed task: method correct but electrode check fails; data still unverified.

lessons.title: P15 — Lining inspection record
lessons.body:
## P15 — Lining inspection record

Use clean coated panels and a suitable verified thickness instrument, plus synthetic environment/cure record: steel 22°C, dew point 20°C, required margin 3°C, DFT 400–600 micrometers, readings 430/570/650. Criteria: (1) verifies instrument/procedure before panel readings; (2) recognizes 2°C failure; (3) recognizes 650 excess; (4)* holds uncured/unverified system from release; (5) documents repair/reinspection. Changed task: environment and thickness pass but cure missing. Do not energize a holiday tester without its safe qualified procedure.

lessons.title: P16 — Mechanism-to-method reasoning
lessons.body:
## P16 — Mechanism-to-method reasoning

Give three records: caustic weld linear indication despite stable thickness; acid dilution followed by accelerated loss; water/sludge pits with unconfirmed microbial hypothesis. Criteria: (1) distinguishes cracking/loss; (2) recognizes chemistry change; (3) does not diagnose MIC from appearance alone; (4)* does not accept a crack from thickness margin; (5) selects suitable evidence/examination/referral. Changed task: apparent external insulation damage; learner plans hidden-surface examination rather than copying the internal mechanism.

lessons.title: P17 — Toughness record
lessons.body:
## P17 — Toughness record

Supply rule mean ≥ 28 J, each ≥ 21 J at−10°C; results 36/29/19 at−10°C. Criteria: (1) traceable material/test identity; (2) mean 28 J; (3)* individual 19 fails; (4) appropriate retest/disposition path; (5) does not equate strength with toughness. Changed task: all energies pass but test temperature wrong. No actual impact-test machine operation is implied.

lessons.title: P18 — Qualification audit
lessons.body:
## P18 — Qualification audit

Use D05 plus production weld map. Criteria: (1) WPS links PQR; (2) supplied thickness/process range checked; (3) welder task/continuity checked; (4)* no invented historical variables/continuity; (5) affected welds held pending evidence. Changed task:28 mm outside range. Award reference-review credit only after learner identifies actual IX and tank requirements in authorized documents.

lessons.title: P19 — NDE report audit
lessons.body:
## P19 — NDE report audit

Use D06 and a synthetic RT technique sheet whose required IQI identification field is blank. Criteria: (1) detects 100 mm coverage gap; (2) identifies missing technique-quality evidence; (3) separates method from acceptance; (4)* does not accept from signatures alone; (5) defines traceable completion/reevaluation. Changed task: full coverage but wrong weld ID. No radiation source is used.

lessons.title: P20 — Repair-detail verification
lessons.body:
## P20 — Repair-detail verification

Use D06's layout and Q20's dimensional nonconformance as two drawing tasks. Criteria: (1) reads specified datums; (2) compares all dimensions; (3) records failed spacing/weld size; (4)* no unauthorized field redesign; (5) rechecks affected requirements after approved revision. Changed task: corrected spacing but undersized actual fillet. Require the as-found record to remain intact.

lessons.title: P21 — Reconstruction traceability
lessons.body:
## P21 — Reconstruction traceability

Use twelve labeled paper shell segments, two without material/location identity and one with documented edge damage. Criteria: (1) complete component map; (2) identifies unknowns; (3) identifies damage independently of identity; (4)* no unsupported reuse approval; (5) new site/service and dossier requirements. Changed task: identify both unknowns but retain edge damage; learner must not close all findings together.

lessons.title: P22 — Test-plan stop response
lessons.body:
## P22 — Test-plan stop response

Use D07 stage log and an unapproved exemption request. Criteria: (1) verifies test basis; (2) calculates water scale correctly; (3)* stops on 11 mm against 8 mm criterion; (4) distinguishes pending exemption from approval; (5) restoration/disposal/records included. Changed task:settlement passes but leak appears. This is a tabletop task, never an actual uncontrolled pressure test.

lessons.title: P23 — Integrated disposition
lessons.body:
## P23 — Integrated disposition

Use D08. Criteria: (1) identifies both level discrepancies; (2) identifies SG exceedance; (3)* holds unsupported release; (4) preserves valid component evidence without misusing it; (5) lists specific owners and verification for closure. Changed task: settings draft corrected but active configuration unverified. Learner must distinguish prepared from verified.

lessons.title: P24 — Final dossier and honest status
lessons.body:
## P24 — Final dossier and honest status

Give a folder containing the learner's station records, one deliberately mislabeled weld report and one open action marked closed. Criteria: (1) finds identity mismatch; (2) restores open status with evidence; (3) retains original/corrected history; (4)* makes no real tank release or external certification claim; (5) produces a usable indexed dossier with limits and next actions. Changed task: a passing retake exists but original failure was deleted; require restoration of the learning audit trail.

lessons.title: Final examination administration
lessons.body:
## Final examination administration

Use the separate controlled Form A in the private instructor directory. It contains 24 original case questions, each requiring 3 scored decisions:72 decisions, 144 points. Allow 150 minutes with calculator and authorized technical references/coursebook; no protected keys, formative-answer sheets, collaboration or external assistance. Pass 116/144 and at least 4/6 in every domain. Any critical unsafe/fabricated-acceptance decision must be corrected and passed on changed reassessment regardless of total. Score each decision 0–2 with the key; accept equivalent defensible wording, require calculations and units. Reasonable accessibility accommodations may change presentation/time, not the competencies being assessed.

After feedback, issue only the affected changed-case prompts from the private reassessment packet. Keep keys protected. Retain original result, instruction delivered, changed response and final disposition. A proctor must not coach during scored work. Never mark the authoring of this exam as an actual learner pass.


---

courses.title: VUC037 | VUC037 explained formative checks

content.title: VUC037 | VUC037 explained formative checks
content.description: Course completion records study only. Certification also requires the separately controlled examination and applicable observed assessments specified in the program. This VNDRLY/U curriculum counterpart does not award, replace, or claim accreditation by the external credential issuer.

lessons.title: VUC037 explained formative checks
lessons.body:
# VUC037 explained formative checks

Attempt each response before reading its answer. Correct every missed answer with a reason, revisit the named chapter and attempt its changed example. These checks teach; they are not the controlled final.

lessons.title: Q01-L1
lessons.body:
## Q01-L1

A drawing belongs to the neighboring tank but matches the apparent diameter. Can it establish this tank’s material?

**Answer:** No. Establish traceability to the actual tank and material record.

**Reason and remediation:** Geometric resemblance does not establish material identity or history. Rebuild the identity sheet. Revisit Q01, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q01-L2
lessons.body:
## Q01-L2

What should a missing material certificate do to an inspection plan?

**Answer:** Identify affected decisions, obtain the authorized investigation or conservative basis, and continue independent observations safely.

**Reason and remediation:** An unknown is neither an automatic pass nor a reason to invent a grade. Revisit Q01, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q02-L1
lessons.body:
## Q02-L1

At unchanged height, what is the head-demand ratio when SG changes from 0.70 to 0.91?

**Answer:** 0.91/0.70 = 1.30, a 30 percent increase.

**Reason and remediation:** Density affects head; this comparison is not a complete service-change approval. Revisit Q02, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q02-L2
lessons.body:
## Q02-L2

Does a doubled pumping rate require only a thickness review?

**Answer:** No; review venting and operating safeguards as well as other affected systems.

**Reason and remediation:** Structural wall capacity does not establish adequate pressure/vacuum protection. Revisit Q02, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q03-L1
lessons.body:
## Q03-L1

Why is “no leak” insufficient evidence for an inaccessible bottom region?

**Answer:** A lack of observed leakage does not establish thickness or absence of deterioration.

**Reason and remediation:** Coverage and detection capability remain unresolved. Revisit Q03, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q03-L2
lessons.body:
## Q03-L2

Name the minimum location information needed to repeat a shell reading.

**Answer:** Tank identity, course/elevation, circumferential position and defined datum or map reference.

**Reason and remediation:** A number without a repeatable location cannot support a reliable trend. Revisit Q03, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q04-L1
lessons.body:
## Q04-L1

The entry permit’s ventilation fails. What happens to the last planned measurement?

**Answer:** Withdraw under the procedure and reassess before re-entry; do not finish the reading first.

**Reason and remediation:** Task completion cannot override entry conditions. Revisit Q04, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q04-L2
lessons.body:
## Q04-L2

A small weld is proposed on connected tank equipment. Why evaluate adjacent equipment?

**Answer:** Vapors or hazardous material can reach the work through connected paths.

**Reason and remediation:** The ignition source is not limited by the physical size of the weld. Revisit Q04, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q05-L1
lessons.body:
## Q05-L1

At velocity 5,900 m/s and round-trip time 1 microsecond, what is thickness?

**Answer:** 2.95 mm.

**Reason and remediation:** Divide velocity times time by two because the pulse travels out and back. Revisit Q05, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q05-L2
lessons.body:
## Q05-L2

A post-use calibration check fails. Is correcting the setting enough?

**Answer:** No; identify affected readings, investigate and repeat required measurements.

**Reason and remediation:** A corrected instrument does not retrospectively validate data. Revisit Q05, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q06-L1
lessons.body:
## Q06-L1

Thickness decreases from 7.2 to 6.6 mm in three years. What is the average rate?

**Answer:** 0.20 mm/year.

**Reason and remediation:** Use comparable actual locations and elapsed time. Revisit Q06, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q06-L2
lessons.body:
## Q06-L2

A measured rate is zero. Is remaining life infinite?

**Answer:** No. Review uncertainty, mechanisms, history and the applicable interval basis.

**Reason and remediation:** Measurement variation and unexamined mechanisms prevent that inference. Revisit Q06, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q07-L1
lessons.body:
## Q07-L1

Why can the whole-course one-foot adjustment not automatically be used for a localized area?

**Answer:** The equation’s height datum and applicability differ.

**Reason and remediation:** Applying the adjustment to the wrong case can create a false acceptance. Revisit Q07, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q07-L2
lessons.body:
## Q07-L2

If future allowance is deducted from measured thickness, should it also be subtracted again in the same net comparison?

**Answer:** No; account for it once using a consistent basis.

**Reason and remediation:** Double counting changes the mathematical meaning; omitting it is also wrong. Revisit Q07, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q08-L1
lessons.body:
## Q08-L1

Can thicker readings outside a thin band be added solely to improve its average?

**Answer:** No. Follow the prescribed area and sampling method.

**Reason and remediation:** Diluting the affected area conceals its condition. Revisit Q08, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q08-L2
lessons.body:
## Q08-L2

Averages pass but a minimum condition fails. What is the result?

**Answer:** Not accepted under that multi-condition rule.

**Reason and remediation:** Every applicable condition must pass; averages cannot cancel minima. Revisit Q08, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q09-L1
lessons.body:
## Q09-L1

Does every MFL application automatically require the same UT confirmation pattern?

**Answer:** No; the qualified procedure and application determine suitable confirmation and sizing.

**Reason and remediation:** Method names do not establish capability or coverage. Revisit Q09, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q09-L2
lessons.body:
## Q09-L2

Why is a remote-bottom minimum not automatically the annular minimum?

**Answer:** Location and configuration can impose different criteria.

**Reason and remediation:** Using the least demanding value everywhere can hide a critical-region failure. Revisit Q09, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q10-L1
lessons.body:
## Q10-L1

Can new sealant alone close a suspected bottom leak finding?

**Answer:** No; establish the source and repair/disposition with evidence.

**Reason and remediation:** Concealing a path is not proving integrity. Revisit Q10, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q10-L2
lessons.body:
## Q10-L2

A new bottom overlies retained material. What must the record preserve?

**Answer:** The actual layers/configuration, protection and detection arrangements and relevant design basis.

**Reason and remediation:** Future inspectors need to understand concealed structures and protection limitations. Revisit Q10, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q11-L1
lessons.body:
## Q11-L1

Why record tank liquid level with a settlement survey?

**Answer:** Loading conditions affect interpretation and comparison.

**Reason and remediation:** Different load states can make otherwise similar readings noncomparable. Revisit Q11, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q11-L2
lessons.body:
## Q11-L2

A benchmark moved. Can its readings prove tank movement?

**Answer:** Not without resolving the datum.

**Reason and remediation:** Reference movement can mimic structural movement. Revisit Q11, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q12-L1
lessons.body:
## Q12-L1

What does a level floating roof prove about all pontoon compartments?

**Answer:** It does not prove every compartment sound or adequate reserve buoyancy.

**Reason and remediation:** A visible position is not a complete integrity assessment. Revisit Q12, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q12-L2
lessons.body:
## Q12-L2

How much fresh-water mass is held by 50 m² at .1 m depth?

**Answer:** 5 m³, approximately 5,000 kg.

**Reason and remediation:** Water accumulation is a meaningful load, not just a housekeeping issue. Revisit Q12, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q13-L1
lessons.body:
## Q13-L1

Can a vent weight be increased to eliminate nuisance opening without review?

**Answer:** No; that changes the device behavior and needs authorized evaluation.

**Reason and remediation:** A nuisance symptom does not authorize altering protection. Revisit Q13, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q13-L2
lessons.body:
## Q13-L2

Two alarms share one failed level transmitter. Are they independent measurements?

**Answer:** No.

**Reason and remediation:** Common dependence can defeat both indications. Revisit Q13, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q14-L1
lessons.body:
## Q14-L1

Does a rectifier power light prove bottom protection?

**Answer:** No.

**Reason and remediation:** Protection depends on actual current distribution, conditions and valid measurements. Revisit Q14, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q14-L2
lessons.body:
## Q14-L2

Does restored cathodic protection replace metal already lost?

**Answer:** No.

**Reason and remediation:** It may control future corrosion but does not restore thickness. Revisit Q14, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q15-L1
lessons.body:
## Q15-L1

A lining is thick enough but uncured. Is it ready for service?

**Answer:** No; cure must meet the approved system requirements.

**Reason and remediation:** Thickness and cure are separate conditions. Revisit Q15, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q15-L2
lessons.body:
## Q15-L2

Why not use any holiday-test voltage that finds defects?

**Answer:** An unsuitable setting can damage the lining or give invalid results.

**Reason and remediation:** Use the approved method and system-specific settings. Revisit Q15, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q16-L1
lessons.body:
## Q16-L1

Stable thickness plus a linear weld indication proves no damage?

**Answer:** No; investigate potential cracking.

**Reason and remediation:** Wall-loss trending does not accept crack-like indications. Revisit Q16, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q16-L2
lessons.body:
## Q16-L2

Can pit appearance alone establish MIC?

**Answer:** No; combine appropriate evidence and alternatives.

**Reason and remediation:** Mechanism attribution requires more than shape. Revisit Q16, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q17-L1
lessons.body:
## Q17-L1

Does tensile strength prove toughness at a low service temperature?

**Answer:** No.

**Reason and remediation:** Strength and resistance to brittle fracture are distinct properties. Revisit Q17, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q17-L2
lessons.body:
## Q17-L2

Why check individual impact values when the mean passes?

**Answer:** The applicable criteria may require both.

**Reason and remediation:** A weak individual result cannot be hidden by averaging. Revisit Q17, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q18-L1
lessons.body:
## Q18-L1

Can a PQR be edited to show values that were intended rather than used?

**Answer:** No.

**Reason and remediation:** It is a record of the actual qualification test. Revisit Q18, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q18-L2
lessons.body:
## Q18-L2

Does a valid WPS prove every welder qualified for the task?

**Answer:** No.

**Reason and remediation:** Procedure and personnel qualifications are separate. Revisit Q18, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q19-L1
lessons.body:
## Q19-L1

Does “per Section V” alone identify every weld acceptance criterion?

**Answer:** No; identify the referencing acceptance standard and applicable requirements.

**Reason and remediation:** Method compliance and acceptance are separate reviews. Revisit Q19, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q19-L2
lessons.body:
## Q19-L2

Can a complete thickness survey replace crack-sensitive weld examination?

**Answer:** Not automatically.

**Reason and remediation:** The technique must be capable of addressing the actual target discontinuity. Revisit Q19, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q20-L1
lessons.body:
## Q20-L1

Why specify whether spacing is edge-to-edge or center-to-center?

**Answer:** They measure different geometric quantities.

**Reason and remediation:** Using the wrong datum can produce a false pass. Revisit Q20, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q20-L2
lessons.body:
## Q20-L2

Can adequate hot-tap spacing alone authorize the operation?

**Answer:** No.

**Reason and remediation:** Material, thickness, contents, conditions and specialist controls also matter. Revisit Q20, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q21-L1
lessons.body:
## Q21-L1

Does moving a tank preserve approval for every new location?

**Answer:** No.

**Reason and remediation:** New site, service and environmental conditions require their applicable review. Revisit Q21, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q21-L2
lessons.body:
## Q21-L2

Why mark plates before dismantling?

**Answer:** To preserve identity, location and material/history traceability.

**Reason and remediation:** Reconstructing records from an unmarked pile can be unreliable. Revisit Q21, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q22-L1
lessons.body:
## Q22-L1

Does a local leak-test pass automatically waive a required hydrotest?

**Answer:** No.

**Reason and remediation:** They have different purposes and exemption conditions. Revisit Q22, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q22-L2
lessons.body:
## Q22-L2

Why not use a pressure-vessel pneumatic ratio on an atmospheric tank?

**Answer:** The tank and test basis differ and dangerous overpressure may result.

**Reason and remediation:** Use a specifically engineered authorized test method. Revisit Q22, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q23-L1
lessons.body:
## Q23-L1

Can several passing components cancel one critical unresolved finding?

**Answer:** No.

**Reason and remediation:** Disposition depends on every applicable condition, not a majority vote. Revisit Q23, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q23-L2
lessons.body:
## Q23-L2

What is the difference between a recommendation and authorization?

**Answer:** A recommendation proposes an action; the designated authority issues the actual decision.

**Reason and remediation:** Reports must not imply authority the author does not have. Revisit Q23, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q24-L1
lessons.body:
## Q24-L1

Does an invoice prove a technical repair action closed?

**Answer:** No.

**Reason and remediation:** Closure requires specified performance, examination and authorization evidence. Revisit Q24, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.

lessons.title: Q24-L2
lessons.body:
## Q24-L2

Should a failed learner attempt be overwritten after a successful retake?

**Answer:** No; retain both and the remediation.

**Reason and remediation:** Credential evidence must reflect the actual learning history. Revisit Q24, identify the assumption you missed and explain a safe corrected decision.


---

courses.title: VUC037 | VUC037 sources and objective coverage

content.title: VUC037 | VUC037 sources and objective coverage
content.description: Course completion records study only. Certification also requires the separately controlled examination and applicable observed assessments specified in the program. This VNDRLY/U curriculum counterpart does not award, replace, or claim accreditation by the external credential issuer.

lessons.title: VUC037 sources and objective coverage
lessons.body:
# VUC037 sources and objective coverage

Author review date: 2026-11-17. The program is VNDRLY-owned instruction, not an API course, API certification or a reproduction of proprietary examinations. Authoritative documents support the technical basis; original synthetic records teach interpretation and decision-making. Controlled references are required resources for the lookup activities. A supplied project criterion is explicitly identified as such and must not be taught as a universal rule.

lessons.title: Edition and source register
lessons.body:
## Edition and source register

S01 — API official API 653 program and linked 2027 BOK/effectivity. Use the edition list in source-review.md, checked against the official one-page effectivity sheet. The 2027 exam basis is distinct from the legally/contractually adopted basis for an operating tank. https://www.api.org/products-and-services/individual-certification-programs/certifications/api653

S02 — API 653 fifth edition with the listed addenda/errata through July 2025. Publisher: https://www.apiwebstore.org/standards/653 . API-authored text inspected at https://studylib.net/doc/28394897/api-653--2025- . This third-party rendering is not the controlled delivery copy. Reference activities require the authorized standard and its actual tables, figures, notes and limits.

S03 — API 653 February 2025 Errata 2, official publisher file: https://ecommiddlewareprod.blob.core.windows.net/webstore/addenda-errata/STD_653_E5_EN_E2.pdf . Relevant corrections include method diameter limit, joint-efficiency applicability, repair approval, a penetration height datum and settlement interpretation. Do not apply an older remembered paragraph without checking these corrections.

S04 — API-authored July 2025 Addendum 4, inspected at https://studylib.net/doc/28428269/std-653-e5-en-a4 . Bottom-examination guidance and personnel/procedure capability matter; old Annex G content was removed. Use the current controlled publication for delivery.

S05 — API 650 fourteenth, August 2025, as listed in the official effectivity sheet. It is the controlled construction/reconstruction reference for the specified activities. A third-party full-text retrieval returned HTTP451; no access bypass was attempted and that text is not claimed reviewed. Authorized reference access is required for the actual table/figure exercises. The BOK is a coverage guide, not a replacement for this standard.

S06 — API RP 575 fifth, September 2024, addenda July 2025/June 2026, verified publisher preview: https://store.accuristech.com/products/preview/2918210 . All text of the official Addendum 1 (11 pages) and Addendum 2 (7 pages) was reviewed. These include Annex D and its amendments. Official files: https://ecommiddlewareprod.blob.core.windows.net/webstore/addenda-errata/RP_575_E5_EN_A1.pdf and https://ecommiddlewareprod.blob.core.windows.net/webstore/addenda-errata/RP_575_E5_EN_A2_Updated.pdf . The base standard is not claimed fully reviewed. The supplementary bottom-qualification case applies the record-review concepts using explicitly synthetic criteria.

S07 — API RP 576 fifth, September 2024, February 2026 addendum; tank vent portions identified in the official effectivity. The BOK contains an inconsistent 6.6 reference on one page versus 6.7 elsewhere. Use the current controlled document and record the discrepancy; do not silently rewrite the source. Sections 4.3.2/6.7 of API-authored fifth-edition text were reviewed at https://studylib.net/doc/28051709/api-rp-576--inspection-of-pressure-relieving-devices-2024 and the official 2026 addendum reviewed at https://ecommiddlewareprod.blob.core.windows.net/webstore/addenda-errata/RP_576_E5_EN_A1.pdf .

S08 — API RP 577 third, October 2020, September 2025 Errata 1. Official errata: https://ecommiddlewareprod.blob.core.windows.net/webstore/addenda-errata/RP_577_E3_EN_E1.pdf . Welding variables and qualification records remain subject to actual applicable IX/tank requirements.

S09 — ASME BPVC V and IX, 2025 editions, as designated by the official effectivity. V supplies examination-method requirements when invoked; applicable tank standards supply their acceptance and additional requirements. Authorized copies are required for actual qualification and NDE reference review. Supplied synthetic qualification ranges in exercises are not universal IX ranges.

S10 — API RP651 fifth, August 2024. Publisher listing https://www.apiwebstore.org/standards/651 . Protection criteria, measurement methods and actual system settings require the controlled reference and competent corrosion review; this packet does not invent a universal potential criterion.

S11 — API RP652 sixth, December 2025. Publisher preview https://store.accuristech.com/products/preview/3040814 . Lining system-specific preparation, application and cure requirements also require the approved manufacturer's instructions.

S12 — API RP571 third, March 2020, mechanism coverage as designated in the official BOK. Mechanism diagnosis must use material/environment/stress/history and suitable examination; synthetic cases are not diagnoses of real assets.

S13 — EPA bulk-container integrity inspection guidance: https://www.epa.gov/oil-spills-prevention-and-preparedness-regulations/spill-prevention-control-and-countermeasure-11 . Determine actual regulatory applicability separately; do not turn guidance into a claim that every asset has the same inspection obligation.

S14 — OSHA permit-required confined spaces: https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.146 . Site-specific evaluation, entry controls and rescue arrangements remain necessary; this course is not an entry permit.

S15 — CSB tank-related hot-work investigations: https://www.csb.gov/recommendations/hot-work-investigations/ . The teaching cases are original and do not claim to reconstruct an investigation.

S16 — HSE floating-roof buoyancy inspection bulletin: https://www.hse.gov.uk/safetybulletins/floating-roof-tanks.htm . Used to support the importance of system condition and maintenance; not a universal design calculation.

S17 — CSB CAPECO final investigation: https://www.csb.gov/caribbean-petroleum-corporation-capeco-refinery-tank-explosion-and-fire/ . Supports the distinction between a displayed level and effective overfill safeguards.

lessons.title: VNDRLY/U Asset Integrity — Damage Mechanisms
lessons.body:
# VNDRLY/U Asset Integrity — Damage Mechanisms

VUC038 · Original teaching material · Available-source learning package, 2026-11-18

lessons.title: What this program teaches
lessons.body:
## What this program teaches

A damage-mechanism review explains how an asset can deteriorate, where that deterioration is likely, what observations would support or contradict the explanation, and what inspection or control is needed. Naming a mechanism is only the start. The learner must connect material, environment, stress and time to a defensible action. This course is for inspectors, corrosion technicians, maintenance engineers and operations personnel who can read equipment drawings, distinguish pressure from temperature, and perform elementary arithmetic. It does not confer API certification, NDE qualification, engineering approval authority or permission to operate damaged equipment.

The available-source basis requested by the user applies. API's public certification page identifies the whole third edition of RP571 as its examination basis. This original VNDRLY program is not a verified reproduction or equivalent of that examination. It uses accessible primary guidance, first-principles instruction and explicitly synthetic records. No unavailable numerical susceptibility boundary is invented. For a live asset, the employer's adopted engineering criteria and qualified specialists control acceptance.

Each chapter contains instruction, a worked decision and a transfer question. Read the explanation before attempting the learning checks. Preserve uncertainty: “credible,” “supported,” “confirmed by the stated evidence,” and “not assessed” mean different things. A mechanism can be credible even when no damage has yet been found. Conversely, finding a pit does not establish its cause.

lessons.title: Q01 — Build an evidence-based mechanism review
lessons.body:
## Q01 — Build an evidence-based mechanism review

Start with the component's identity and history: alloy and heat treatment, fabrication and repairs, fluid phases and contaminants, operating and transient temperatures, pressures, loads, time in service and prior inspections. Use actual conditions rather than a nominal process-flow diagram. A dry stream at the unit inlet can become wet in a cooler; a continuously hot line can spend shutdowns wet and exposed to air. A replacement spool can differ from the original metallurgy.

For each candidate mechanism write four things: the required conditions, the susceptible locations, the evidence presently available and the missing evidence that could change the decision. Then select a detection method and mitigation appropriate to that candidate. Do not eliminate a mechanism just because the last inspection did not look for it. “Not detected” is meaningful only with a method, coverage, sensitivity and date. Process changes after that date can invalidate the inference.

Separate prevention, detection and consequence control. A coating can reduce contact with an environment; a thickness survey can detect some wall loss; isolation and emergency response can reduce exposure after a leak. One does not replace the others. Assign an owner and due date to each unresolved condition. A risk ranking helps prioritize work, but cannot convert unknown wall condition into acceptable wall condition.

**Worked decision.** A line register says dry gas; startup records show water flushing and a low point without drainage. Internal aqueous corrosion remains credible during wet periods. Request the flushing chemistry, drainage record and low-point inspection, rather than marking all internal corrosion “not applicable.”

**Transfer.** The drain is now installed. What closes the old exposure? Installation prevents some future retention; it does not remove existing damage. A baseline examination and approved disposition are still needed.

lessons.title: Q02 — Read materials and microstructure correctly
lessons.body:
## Q02 — Read materials and microstructure correctly

Carbon steel, low-alloy steel, austenitic stainless steel, duplex stainless steel, nickel alloys, copper alloys and cast irons do not respond identically to the same service. Composition controls only part of the response. Heat treatment, grain structure, cold work, weld zones, inclusions and hardness can change susceptibility. A material test report must be traceable to the actual component; a nearby component's certificate is not evidence for it.

Positive material identification can help establish alloy chemistry within the capabilities of the instrument. It does not automatically establish carbon content, heat treatment, toughness, strength, sensitization or freedom from cracks. A hardness test answers a different question from chemical analysis. Metallography examines structure; mechanical tests examine selected properties. Specify the property that must be established before selecting a test.

Austenitic stainless steel resists many environments that attack carbon steel, but it is not universally corrosion-proof. Duplex performance depends on an appropriate phase balance and fabrication history. Cast iron may retain its shape after selective attack has weakened the metallic matrix. A high-alloy repair can also create a dissimilar-metal interface requiring separate review.

**Worked decision.** Handheld chemistry identifies a stainless family on a replacement nozzle, but its weld history is missing. The result supports composition identification only. It does not close a concern about heat-affected-zone structure or cracking. Obtain the fabrication record and select the necessary property or flaw examination.

**Transfer.** Why is “upgrade everything to stainless” not a mechanism review? It can exchange one vulnerability for another, leave fabrication defects unaddressed and ignore the actual environment.

lessons.title: Q03 — General corrosion, localized attack and measurement
lessons.body:
## Q03 — General corrosion, localized attack and measurement

In aqueous corrosion, anodic metal dissolution and cathodic reactions are coupled through the metal and electrolyte. Changes in chemistry, oxygen, temperature, deposits and flow change local conditions. General loss spreads across an area; localized attack concentrates loss. A component can have both. An average thickness can conceal a deep pit or a narrow groove.

For a like-for-like measurement, average loss rate equals thickness loss divided by elapsed time. Establish that both readings refer to the same location, method and surface condition. A negative apparent rate is not metal regeneration; check measurement uncertainty, location and records. If service changed, the historic average may not represent future behavior. Neither a linear rate nor a remaining-life arithmetic exercise is an automatic inspection interval or fitness-for-service decision.

Pits can create locally aggressive chemistry. Crevices restrict transport and may develop conditions unlike the bulk fluid. Inspect gasket interfaces, lap joints, deposits and stagnant regions. Clean surfaces only under an approved safe procedure and preserve evidence when failure analysis is needed. The deepest remaining ligament and the geometry of the affected area may matter more than the mean value.

**Worked decision.** Matched readings fall from 8.0 to 7.4 mm in two years: average loss is 0.30 mm/year. A mapped pit at 4.1 mm is not represented by that rate. Record the pit separately and obtain the applicable localized-damage assessment.

**Transfer.** A new survey reads 7.6 mm at the original spot. Reconcile instrument, position and uncertainty before using the apparent increase to lengthen any interval.

lessons.title: Q04 — Atmospheric, soil and under-insulation corrosion
lessons.body:
## Q04 — Atmospheric, soil and under-insulation corrosion

External corrosion depends on exposure as well as alloy. Water, salts, coating defects, soil conditions and wet/dry cycles can produce sharply different behavior along one line. Insulation can conceal water entry and damage. Weather seals, penetrations, supports, low points and termination details deserve particular attention. A sound outer jacket does not prove that the metal beneath it is dry.

Carbon steel under wet insulation can lose wall. Stainless steel under contaminated wet insulation can develop localized attack or chloride stress corrosion cracking. The consequence is that a thickness-only inspection strategy may be incomplete. Screening techniques can prioritize areas, but their limitations and required follow-up must be explicit. Removal of insulation is itself work requiring access, contamination and process-temperature controls.

Buried systems require a separate understanding of coating condition, electrical interference, soil exposure and any cathodic protection system. An aboveground reading does not establish the condition of a soil-to-air transition or the full buried run. Cathodic protection readings need a defined method, valid reference electrode and qualified interpretation; one favorable reading is not blanket proof of protection.

**Worked decision.** A stainless line has failed weather seals and saline deposits at a support. A few satisfactory spot thickness readings do not eliminate cracking. Plan an appropriate surface/crack examination with qualified personnel and investigate the water source.

**Transfer.** If the jacket is repaired today, why retain inspection follow-up? Weatherproofing addresses entry of new water, not the existing metal condition or retained contaminants.

lessons.title: Q05 — Galvanic, crevice and selective corrosion
lessons.body:
## Q05 — Galvanic, crevice and selective corrosion

Galvanic corrosion requires an electrical connection between dissimilar electrochemical surfaces and an electrolyte. The relative areas and local exposure matter: a small anodic area coupled to a large cathodic area can suffer concentrated attack. Merely listing two alloy names is insufficient; determine electrical continuity, electrolyte contact and geometry. Coating choices must consider defects and the resulting exposed-area ratio.

Crevice attack arises from restricted local exchange, not necessarily a dissimilar-metal pair. A nonmetallic gasket can create a crevice. Selective corrosion removes or changes particular constituents of an alloy, leaving a weakened residue. Dezincification can affect susceptible brasses; graphitic corrosion can weaken cast iron while preserving a deceptively recognizable shape. Distinguish graphitic corrosion from high-temperature graphitization of steel, which is a microstructural change.

Detection must test the suspected weakness. Color, dimensions or a superficial tap are not adequate acceptance evidence. A specialist may require sectioning, metallography, chemistry and property evaluation. Repair or replacement must address the environment and coupling, not only restore appearance.

**Worked decision.** A brass component shows a porous copper-colored region and seepage. Treat selective attack as a candidate and preserve a representative sample. A coating over the outside does not restore the lost load-bearing alloy.

**Transfer.** A stainless patch is proposed on a carbon steel vessel. Review the joint, electrolyte exposure and area relationship as well as welding and design requirements; “more noble” does not mean every adjacent surface benefits.

lessons.title: Q06 — Cooling water, deposits and microbiological influence
lessons.body:
## Q06 — Cooling water, deposits and microbiological influence

Cooling-water damage can include general corrosion, pitting, under-deposit attack, erosion-assisted loss, fouling and microbiologically influenced corrosion. Water chemistry at a clean sample point may differ from chemistry beneath a deposit or in a stagnant branch. Flow distribution, temperature, treatment history, leakage and intermittent operation influence local conditions.

Microorganisms can influence electrochemical conditions, deposits and local chemistry. A positive microbial test alone does not establish that MIC caused the damage; microorganisms may be present without being the controlling cause. Conversely, a negative bulk-water sample does not eliminate activity beneath an established deposit. Combine morphology, deposits, local sampling, process history and expert interpretation. Preserve samples promptly using the laboratory's specified collection and transport procedure.

Treatment is a controlled operating activity. Do not improvise biocide additions, mix chemicals or mechanically disturb suspect deposits on live equipment. Corrective measures can include approved cleaning, treatment control, stagnation reduction and material changes, each checked for unintended consequences. Monitor both the treatment and the asset response.

**Worked decision.** A heat exchanger has rising pressure drop, patchy deposits and clustered pits. The defensible conclusion is a set of candidates requiring evidence, not “MIC confirmed.” Map the damage, review treatment interruptions and arrange representative deposit and metal examination.

**Transfer.** A clean water sample after a chemical treatment does not prove the old deposit-covered surface is sound. Establish its condition separately.

lessons.title: Q07 — Carbon dioxide, oxygen and sour-water environments
lessons.body:
## Q07 — Carbon dioxide, oxygen and sour-water environments

Carbon dioxide dissolved in water can create corrosive conditions for susceptible steels. Water availability, temperature, pressure, chemistry, flow and protective-film behavior influence the result. Dry CO2 and wet CO2 service are not interchangeable. Oxygen ingress can introduce or accelerate other reactions. Do not assume a small oxygen measurement at one location describes an entire intermittent system.

Sour water introduces sulfur species and may introduce hydrogen-related cracking concerns as well as metal loss. pH, contaminants and local concentration matter. A fluid described simply as “sour” does not identify the controlling mechanism. Distinguish general or localized aqueous corrosion from blistering, hydrogen-induced cracking, stress-oriented hydrogen-induced cracking and sulfide stress cracking. The inspection plan must consider each credible form separately.

Corrosion coupons and probes provide useful local evidence, but may not represent deposits, phase separation or cracking. Record where they are installed and what they measure. Inhibitor performance must be evaluated against the actual distribution and operating envelope, including startup, shutdown and interruptions.

**Worked decision.** A gas line normally runs dry but collects water at a low point during winter. An upstream coupon with low loss cannot clear that low point. Confirm liquid composition and retention, inspect the susceptible location and review drainage controls.

**Transfer.** Increasing an inhibitor dose is not proof that a crack-like indication has been arrested or made acceptable; obtain the required integrity assessment.

lessons.title: Q08 — Acid, caustic and chemical-service corrosion
lessons.body:
## Q08 — Acid, caustic and chemical-service corrosion

Chemical names alone do not determine compatibility. Concentration, temperature, contaminants, aeration, velocity and phase determine whether a material is suitable. Dilution can change corrosivity in unexpected ways, so neither “weaker acid” nor “lower concentration” automatically means safer service. Mixing and injection zones may experience a chemistry absent from the bulk stream.

Hydrochloric, sulfuric, hydrofluoric, phosphoric and organic-acid services need service-specific review. HF service also introduces serious personnel hazards and possible hydrogen-related damage concerns in susceptible materials. This course does not authorize sampling, opening or repairing those systems. Caustic service can cause thinning and stress corrosion cracking; local concentration beneath deposits or during evaporation can be important even when the bulk concentration appears modest.

Inspect injection hardware, mixing zones, drains, deadlegs and phase-change locations. Establish the correct corrosion-control and materials specialist before selecting an alloy or changing chemistry. A compatibility chart without its concentration and temperature basis is not a design approval.

**Worked decision.** An injection quill is shortened during repair and downstream localized thinning appears. Investigate mixing and impingement together with chemistry; replacing only the thinned spool leaves the changed exposure in place.

**Transfer.** A proposed water flush must be reviewed for reaction heat, dilution effects, waste handling and trapped chemical. A classroom example is not a flushing instruction.

lessons.title: Q09 — Ammonium salts, sour-water concentration and amines
lessons.body:
## Q09 — Ammonium salts, sour-water concentration and amines

Ammonium chloride and ammonium bisulfide problems require attention to deposition, water availability, concentration and flow. A deposit can hide an aggressive local environment. The location where a salt forms or becomes wet can differ from the location of a bulk stream sample. Changes in feed contaminants, wash-water distribution or exchanger temperature can move the susceptible zone.

Separate salt deposition and fouling from corrosion underneath deposits and from high-velocity corrosive attack. A pressure-drop increase can signal fouling, but is not a metal-thickness measurement. Wash-water control requires an engineered basis; simply adding water can introduce other problems if mixing and distribution are inadequate.

Amine systems can experience corrosion and cracking influenced by solvent condition, contaminants, temperature, loading and fabrication stress. A general corrosion reading does not clear weld-related cracking. Record solution analyses, operating excursions, reclaiming/treatment history and weld examination coverage. Mitigation must address the system conditions and the existing damage.

**Worked decision.** After a feed change, an exchanger outlet has deposits and localized loss while its upstream coupon remains stable. Revisit the deposition and wetting model and inspect the affected exchanger and downstream region. Do not average away the local result.

**Transfer.** Cleaning restores flow but does not establish remaining integrity. Obtain post-cleaning examination and a controlled disposition.

lessons.title: Q10 — Sulfidation and naphthenic-acid corrosion
lessons.body:
## Q10 — Sulfidation and naphthenic-acid corrosion

Hot sulfur-containing process streams can attack susceptible alloys. Material composition, temperature and stream chemistry matter. Components within one circuit may behave differently, especially when material history is mixed. The Chevron Richmond investigation illustrates why measurements on selected fittings cannot automatically represent every pipe component. [S03]

Naphthenic-acid corrosion is another high-temperature process concern. Acid characteristics, temperature, velocity, phase and metallurgy interact; a single total-acid-number result is not a complete prediction. Sulfidation and acid attack can coexist or interact, so the review should not force every observation into one category. Examine locations of turbulence and phase change along with apparently uniform runs.

A thickness plan should follow actual component boundaries and credible attack locations. Material verification helps define groups but does not measure damage. Changes in crude blend or operating conditions require review of the inspection and control basis. An alloy upgrade must be justified for all credible mechanisms, including welds and transition pieces.

**Worked decision.** Four fittings remain near original thickness, but the intervening pipe has unknown chemistry. The fittings are not adequate proof of the pipe's condition. Establish the pipe components and examine them using the required coverage rather than extrapolating from a favorable sample.

**Transfer.** A new feed has the same sulfur content but different acid and boiling characteristics. Explain why the old mechanism review must be revisited rather than copied unchanged.

lessons.title: Q11 — Oxidation, hot corrosion and carburizing environments
lessons.body:
## Q11 — Oxidation, hot corrosion and carburizing environments

At elevated temperature, metal can react with gases to form surface scales. Whether a scale protects depends on composition, adherence and service conditions. Thermal cycling can disrupt a protective layer. High-temperature corrosion may therefore accelerate after a process or temperature change even without an aqueous electrolyte.

Oxidation, fuel-ash corrosion and hot-gas attack require attention to deposits, gas composition and metal temperature. Carburization introduces carbon into susceptible material and can change properties. Decarburization removes carbon from affected regions. Metal dusting is a distinct form of severe degradation in suitable carbonaceous environments; it is not simply loose external dirt. Nitriding can alter surface and near-surface properties in nitrogen-bearing service. These mechanisms need material-specific review rather than a single generic “heat damage” diagnosis.

Use temperature history, gas/deposit analysis, thickness or dimensional data and appropriate metallurgical examination. An infrared image is useful only with its emissivity, line-of-sight and operating context; it is not a direct measurement of internal microstructure. Repairing insulation or refractory may address overheating but does not reverse existing material degradation.

**Worked decision.** A furnace tube has changed diameter and an unusual surface layer after a firing imbalance. Establish actual tube-metal exposure and request metallurgical evaluation. Removing scale and measuring one wall point cannot establish retained mechanical properties.

**Transfer.** Normal process outlet temperature does not rule out a local hot spot. Identify what measurements describe the metal itself.

lessons.title: Q12 — Dew-point corrosion and shutdown exposure
lessons.body:
## Q12 — Dew-point corrosion and shutdown exposure

Cooling a gas stream can create a liquid phase with a chemistry far more aggressive than the bulk gas. Dew-point corrosion depends on the condensate composition and surface temperature, not merely the average gas temperature. Cold spots, air leakage, insulation defects and startup/shutdown transients can move the condensation region.

Acidic condensate in combustion or process systems can cause localized attack. A dry-service designation during normal operation does not clear shutdown conditions. Shutdown can also admit oxygen and moisture to deposits formed during operation, enabling different mechanisms such as polythionic-acid stress corrosion cracking in susceptible sensitized stainless materials.

Review the entire operating cycle: startup, steady service, upset, wash, steam-out, cooling, opening, storage and restart. Controls must be engineered for the particular service and applied before the damaging exposure occurs. An improvised neutralization or purge instruction can create serious hazards; use approved procedures and trained personnel.

**Worked decision.** A duct wall corrodes at a cold support while the gas temperature remains above its normal target. The wall temperature and local condensation conditions matter. Inspect the cold region, investigate gas chemistry and heat loss, and review the control basis.

**Transfer.** If a unit was sound before shutdown but exposed to wet air afterward, the old inspection date does not automatically cover the new exposure.

lessons.title: Q13 — Stress corrosion cracking: the three-part interaction
lessons.body:
## Q13 — Stress corrosion cracking: the three-part interaction

Stress corrosion cracking requires a susceptible material condition, an environment capable of causing the mechanism and tensile stress. Residual fabrication stress can matter even when operating pressure is low. Cracks can be transgranular, intergranular or mixed depending on the system; no single crack path identifies every SCC mechanism.

Chlorides can threaten susceptible stainless steels; caustic, carbonate, amine, ammonia and other environments require their own material-specific reviews. Do not treat all SCC as chloride cracking or assume all stainless grades behave alike. Local concentration and weld condition often matter more than a bulk sample or nominal alloy description.

Cracking can be serious with little general wall loss. Select techniques capable of finding the expected crack orientation and depth, with qualified procedures and coverage. Surface methods do not necessarily size through-wall extent. Volumetric methods have geometry and material limitations. The responsible specialist must connect detection capability to the required integrity decision.

**Worked decision.** A welded ammonia-service vessel has satisfactory thickness but new linear indications near welds. Thickness is not a clearance for SCC. Escalate the indications, examine relevant weld regions and review service chemistry and residual-stress history. OSHA's pressure-vessel guidance identifies ammonia-service cracking as a distinct concern. [S05]

**Transfer.** Why might a low operating stress not eliminate the concern? Fabrication and repair can leave tensile residual stresses that the operating-pressure calculation does not represent.

lessons.title: Q14 — Wet hydrogen damage: blistering, HIC, SOHIC and SSC
lessons.body:
## Q14 — Wet hydrogen damage: blistering, HIC, SOHIC and SSC

Hydrogen generated at a metal surface can enter susceptible steel. In wet sour environments, several different damage forms may be credible. Blistering involves internal accumulation and separation. Hydrogen-induced cracking can develop along internal features and link. Stress-oriented hydrogen-induced cracking describes arrays associated with stress. Sulfide stress cracking involves susceptible material and tensile stress in the sour environment. These are related concerns, not interchangeable labels.

Material cleanliness, hardness, weld condition, stress and environment influence susceptibility. A material certificate identifying grade does not prove that every weld or repair satisfies the applicable service requirements. Hardness screening answers only part of the question. A thickness reading may miss internal separations or cracking.

Select examination to match the candidate morphology and location. An ultrasonic approach intended for wall thickness is not automatically a qualified HIC or crack assessment. Record coverage around welds, heat-affected zones and plate regions as applicable. Avoid drilling, grinding or heating an unexplained blister on operating equipment; escalation and a controlled inspection plan come first.

**Worked decision.** A sour-water vessel has a bulge and internally aligned ultrasonic indications. Do not describe it merely as corrosion allowance consumption. Establish whether hydrogen-related separation and cracking are present and obtain the required engineering disposition.

**Transfer.** A new lower-hardness weld procedure can reduce a future susceptibility; it does not remove existing internal cracking from adjacent plate.

lessons.title: Q15 — High-temperature hydrogen attack
lessons.body:
## Q15 — High-temperature hydrogen attack

High-temperature hydrogen attack is different from wet sour cracking and ordinary corrosion thinning. Hydrogen can react within susceptible steel, degrading its microstructure and developing internal damage. Temperature, hydrogen partial pressure, exposure time, material and stress history matter. Use actual hydrogen partial pressure rather than total system pressure alone.

The Tesoro Anacortes investigation demonstrated the consequences of missed HTHA in a carbon-steel exchanger. It also shows why a historic screening assumption or ordinary thickness readings should not be treated as definitive clearance. [S04] A chart boundary is not a substitute for verifying the material, actual exposure and limitations of the assessment method.

Specialized inspection needs an appropriate procedure, qualified personnel, suitable calibration/validation and a documented understanding of detection limits. No single classroom description makes an operator qualified to diagnose HTHA. Metallurgical confirmation may be needed. Once degradation has occurred, reducing temperature does not restore the original microstructure.

**Worked decision.** A process stream is 60% hydrogen at 100 bar absolute total pressure. The simple gas-mixture estimate is 60 bar absolute hydrogen partial pressure, subject to the engineering model's assumptions. Using 100 bar gauge or a stale composition would misstate the basis. This calculation does not establish a safe operating limit.

**Transfer.** A normal thickness result after an excursion does not establish absence of internal HTHA. Specify the missing assessment rather than calling the equipment safe.

lessons.title: Q16 — Fatigue, vibration and corrosion fatigue
lessons.body:
## Q16 — Fatigue, vibration and corrosion fatigue

Fatigue develops under repeated stress cycles. Local stress concentration, weld details, supports, vibration, starts/stops and operating changes can matter more than the nominal average load. Crack initiation and growth can occur without appreciable general corrosion. A static strength calculation alone does not address fatigue life.

Mechanical vibration can drive many small cycles, particularly at small-bore connections, unsupported attachments and rotating-equipment interfaces. Thermal cycling can also produce fatigue when parts expand differently or a temperature gradient repeatedly changes. Corrosion fatigue combines cyclic stress with a damaging environment; an air-based fatigue assumption may not represent that service.

Identify the load source and cycle history, inspect susceptible details with suitable crack methods and correct the initiating condition. A weld repair without correcting resonance, support or thermal mixing may fail again. Temporary bracing or grinding requires engineering control; it is not an improvised field cure.

**Worked decision.** A small-bore drain repeatedly cracks after a pump operating change. Rewelding it a third time is not a complete response. Evaluate vibration and support, characterize the crack, inspect similar connections and obtain an engineered correction.

**Transfer.** Why can a short upset matter even when daily averages are normal? Peak stress and cycle count are concealed by an average, and fatigue depends on the repeated local stress history.

lessons.title: Q17 — Creep, stress rupture and thermal distortion
lessons.body:
## Q17 — Creep, stress rupture and thermal distortion

Creep is time-dependent deformation under sustained load at elevated temperature. Material condition, metal temperature, stress and time govern its significance. Stress rupture is a possible end result. Bulging, dimensional changes or microstructural evidence may indicate concern, but absence of a visible bulge does not establish remaining life.

Local overheating can sharply change the exposure of a tube or component. Process-fluid temperature is not necessarily the highest metal temperature. Deposits, flame impingement, refractory defects and loss of cooling can create hot regions. Compare operating history with the design and material basis using qualified engineering analysis rather than a generic maximum-temperature rule.

Assessment may require dimensional survey, thickness, metallography, hardness and other specialized evidence. Each method has limits. Surface replication samples a particular area and does not automatically describe the full wall or all components. Record the locations and relation to the hottest or most highly stressed regions.

**Worked decision.** Two heater tubes have identical outlet-fluid temperature, but one has heavy internal deposit and measurable bowing. They do not have equivalent thermal evidence. Investigate local metal temperature and degradation before assigning the same remaining-life conclusion.

**Transfer.** Restoring firing balance prevents some future exposure but cannot undo accumulated creep damage; the condition assessment remains necessary.

lessons.title: Q18 — Embrittlement, phase changes and brittle fracture
lessons.body:
## Q18 — Embrittlement, phase changes and brittle fracture

Some damage mechanisms reduce toughness or ductility without large wall loss. Temper embrittlement, sigma-phase formation, 475°C embrittlement, strain aging and other material-specific changes depend on alloy, thermal history and structure. Their names are not universal temperature limits. A mechanism review must establish whether the actual material and exposure can support the proposed change.

Brittle fracture is a failure mode involving inadequate resistance to crack propagation under the applied conditions. Temperature, toughness, flaw size, constraint, thickness and stress matter. A pressure test can introduce a hazardous combination rather than prove all future conditions safe. Follow the approved testing and minimum-temperature basis.

Graphitization in susceptible steels is a high-temperature microstructural concern and differs from selective graphitic corrosion of cast iron. Spheroidization and softening may change strength in affected steels. Identify which property is at risk and choose the corresponding examination or test. Hardness alone is not a universal toughness measurement.

**Worked decision.** A thick older vessel is scheduled for pressurization during unusually cold weather. A recent thickness survey does not establish brittle-fracture resistance. Confirm the material, flaw and temperature assessment and approved operating/test limits before proceeding.

**Transfer.** An alloy identification result does not establish that a long thermal exposure has left its original toughness unchanged.

lessons.title: Q19 — Erosion, cavitation, impingement and FAC
lessons.body:
## Q19 — Erosion, cavitation, impingement and FAC

Mechanical removal by particles or droplets, bubble-collapse damage and chemically assisted wall loss can produce similar-looking thinning but require different controls. Erosion concentrates where flow and geometry direct damaging contact. Cavitation involves vapor formation and collapse under suitable pressure conditions. Flashing, impingement and two-phase flow deserve distinct process review.

Flow-accelerated corrosion involves dissolution and transport of a protective surface film in susceptible water/steam service; it should not be reduced to mechanical abrasion.
