lessons.title: Crosswalk
lessons.body:
## Crosswalk

Situation awareness: Q02/Q03, W01/W04, P02/P03. Decision-making: Q04, W03, P04. Communication: Q05/Q06, W02, P05/P06. Teamwork: Q07, W03, P07. Leadership: Q08, W03/P08. Performance factors: Q09/Q10, W05, P09/P10. Q01 establishes systems context; Q11 develops debrief/learning; Q12 integrates the skills through I78. Each of 12 domains has two explained formative checks, a controlled final case and a changed independent reassessment.

All scenarios, volumes, duty logs, response cards and behavioral rubrics are original. The scenario's SIM-SECURE/SIM-HOLD/SIM-RESUME labels are classroom states, not field operating instructions. Observed role-play is sufficient for this nontechnical scope; it cannot be substituted for a technical well-control practical. Critical unsafe decisions fail regardless of fluency or aggregate score. Personality, accent and seniority are not competence measures. No account creation, purchase, publication or software work is required to complete these materials.

courses.title: VUC079 | VNDRLY/U Well Control Awareness

content.title: VUC079 | VNDRLY/U Well Control Awareness
content.description: Course completion records study only. Certification also requires the separately controlled examination and applicable observed assessments specified in the program. This VNDRLY/U curriculum counterpart does not award, replace, or claim accreditation by the external credential issuer.

lessons.title: VNDRLY/U Well Control Awareness
lessons.body:
# VNDRLY/U Well Control Awareness

Program VUC079 · Original materials · 18 November 2026

For new entrants, ancillary workers and others who need to recognize well-control concerns. No prior well-control qualification is required. Basic reading and arithmetic support are provided. This is a VNDRLY awareness award, not an IWCF certificate or operator/supervisor authorization.

Outcomes: explain the well life cycle; trace a simplified circulation path; interpret a static pressure example; recognize an unexplained warning; identify containment and intervention boundaries; communicate and follow the site emergency plan. Ten teaching chapters support these outcomes. All numbers, well identifiers and operational cards below are fictional.

lessons.title: Q79-01 — The well, the industry and your role
lessons.body:
## Q79-01 — The well, the industry and your role

Oil and gas occur in pore spaces and fractures within rock, not necessarily in an underground cavern. Exploration estimates whether a resource is present; appraisal reduces uncertainty; development provides wells and facilities; production brings fluids to surface for processing and transport. Water can be produced with hydrocarbons. An unexpected fluid movement matters even when nobody sees flames or smells gas. Well control protects people, the environment and the installation by keeping subsurface fluids within intended boundaries.

A well connects pressure sources at depth to equipment and people at surface. A production target, a reservoir estimate and a safe operating envelope are different information. A new employee may know the name of the reservoir without knowing its pressure. Missing information is a reason to ask the responsible person, not to assume a familiar well is harmless.

Your awareness role is to recognize a condition that may threaten control, communicate what you observed, and follow the emergency instructions for your assigned role. It is not to decide a kill method, close an unfamiliar valve, adjust mud density or issue a restart. Stop your own unsafe activity and raise the alarm through the site procedure. Do not wait for mathematical certainty before reporting an obvious warning. Know the well identifier, supervisor, alarm method and muster location before entering the work area.

Worked situation: a delivery driver sees liquid escaping from a line near a wellhead. The driver should stay clear, notify the designated contact with location and observation, and follow instructions from a safe position. Calling it water because it looks clear is an unsupported diagnosis. Driving through the release to avoid delaying the job creates another exposure.

Changed application: the release stops before the supervisor arrives. Report the time and location anyway; an intermittent symptom is still evidence. Record what was seen rather than claiming the well is safe. A useful report distinguishes observation, uncertainty and requested response.

lessons.title: Q79-02 — Well life cycle and changing barriers
lessons.body:
## Q79-02 — Well life cycle and changing barriers

A typical well passes through planning, construction, completion, production, intervention, suspension and permanent abandonment. The order can include repeated interventions and changed uses. Construction creates the borehole and installs casing and cement. Completion equips the well for its intended flow path. Production operates that path within a managed envelope. Intervention investigates or changes an existing well. Suspension leaves a well for later work; abandonment establishes permanent isolation under the applicable design and regulatory requirements.

A barrier is a means of preventing unintended flow along a particular path. A fluid column, casing, cement, packer, plug and valve may contribute to a barrier system when suitable and verified for the actual condition. Merely naming two items does not demonstrate two independent barriers. They may share a failure path, be in the wrong location or lack evidence of integrity. Awareness learners identify the intended path and ask for the current verified barrier status; competent personnel determine the design and acceptance criteria.

A barrier drawing must match the current operation. Removing tubing, opening an access point or changing fluid can alter what contains pressure. A signature from the previous shift does not prove the configuration remains unchanged. Handover should identify the well, current operation, barrier status, unresolved issues, prohibited actions and the person responsible for the next decision.

Worked situation: a suspended well has a locked surface valve and a drawing showing a downhole plug. The plug verification field is blank. Do not translate the drawing into a claim that both barriers were tested. Ask the responsible supervisor to resolve the evidence before the planned access work. A lock can prevent casual operation but cannot establish the integrity of every flow path.

Changed application: the plug record is found, but it names a different well. The evidence mismatch remains. Correct the identity and configuration before relying on it. Long inactivity, low production and a clean exterior are not proof of zero stored energy.

lessons.title: Q79-03 — Reading a rig and its circulation path
lessons.body:
## Q79-03 — Reading a rig and its circulation path

Land rigs, jack-ups, fixed offshore installations and floating units place equipment in different environments. A floating installation adds movement and marine interfaces; it is not simply a land rig placed on water. At awareness level, identify the work areas, controlled access, alarm arrangements and escape routes rather than assuming equipment locations from a familiar site.

In a simplified conventional drilling circuit, fluid travels from the active tanks through pumps and the drillstring, exits near the bit, and returns through the annulus to surface processing and tanks. The annulus is the space outside the pipe and inside the surrounding hole or casing. Cuttings are carried upward with the returning fluid. Transfers between tanks and additions to the system affect the measured volume. These activities must be communicated so that an unexplained change is not hidden by an assumed transfer.

Separate the hoisting, rotating, circulating and pressure-control functions. A derrick or mast supports lifting operations; the rotary system turns the string; pumps circulate fluid; pressure-control equipment supports containment when the approved operation requires it. Knowing a component's name is not permission to enter its danger zone. Suspended loads, moving pipe, high-pressure lines and rotating equipment create hazards independent of the well's pressure balance.

Worked situation: a simplified drawing labels A active tank, B pump, C drillpipe, D bit, E annulus, F solids processing. Trace A-B-C-D-E-F-A. A learner who traces the normal return through the drillpipe has reversed the conventional classroom model. Actual reverse-circulation and specialist operations require different approved diagrams; do not apply this diagram universally.

Changed application: the drawing is for a subsea installation, but the induction map shows only a land muster point. Request the correct installation instructions before access. The pressure-control location and emergency routes cannot be inferred from a generic training sketch.

lessons.title: Q79-04 — Pressure, depth and the limits of a simple model
lessons.body:
## Q79-04 — Pressure, depth and the limits of a simple model

Pressure is force per unit area. Hydrostatic pressure is produced by the weight of a fluid column. In this course's uniform, static liquid model, pressure in psi equals 0.052 multiplied by density in pounds per gallon multiplied by vertical fluid height in feet. The factor is specific to these units. Use true vertical height, not the longer distance measured along a deviated well. State units and assumptions before calculating.

Worked model: a full 4,000 ft vertical column of 10 ppg liquid gives 0.052 × 10 × 4,000 = 2,080 psi. A 5,000 ft measured pipe path to the same vertical depth does not give 2,600 psi of hydrostatic head. If the liquid level drops by 500 vertical ft, the remaining 3,500 ft column gives 1,820 psi. The lost head is 260 psi. These are teaching calculations, not a fluid program or a safe work limit.

Compare pressure at the same depth and on the same reference basis. A gauge at surface is not automatically the pressure at the reservoir. Gas, mixed fluids, temperature, flow friction, surface pressure and transients can make the simple model inadequate. A correct calculation from incomplete inputs can still support a wrong decision. Report the limitation rather than concealing it behind extra decimal places.

Too little wellbore pressure relative to a communicating formation can permit an influx. Excessive pressure can cause losses or other damage. The answer is not always to make the fluid heavier. Qualified personnel evaluate the operating window and the actual condition. The awareness learner does not prescribe a density or pressure setting.

Changed model: 11 ppg and 3,000 ft produce 1,716 psi. At 2,800 ft the result is 1,601.6 psi, a reduction of 114.4 psi. Explain the reduction, then identify why this alone cannot establish whether a real well is safe. No formation pressure, dynamic condition or approved envelope has been supplied.

lessons.title: Q79-05 — How an influx can develop
lessons.body:
## Q79-05 — How an influx can develop

An influx is unintended entry of formation fluid into the well. It may involve gas, oil or water. A kick is not synonymous with a visible blowout: an early indication may exist while the system still contains the fluids. A blowout involves loss of control. Prevention and early recognition matter because waiting for an obvious release sacrifices time and control options.

Pressure can become inadequate because the fluid density is unsuitable, the well is not kept full, fluid is lost, formation pressure differs from the forecast, or movement creates a temporary reduction in pressure. Pulling pipe can create a swabbing effect; running pipe can create a pressure increase known as surge. These are reasons to follow the approved movement and monitoring procedure, not instructions to improvise a tripping speed. An apparently adequate static calculation does not eliminate transient effects.

Gas can expand as pressure falls. A small amount at depth can occupy more space nearer surface. Do not use this general principle to forecast a real kick's size without the appropriate model. The practical awareness consequence is that a small early warning deserves attention; it is not safe to wait for a large tank gain or visible gas cloud.

Worked situation: the crew believes the fluid density is correct, but returns are being lost and the fluid level may fall. Correct density alone cannot preserve the head of a column that is no longer full. The learner reports the losses and uncertainty immediately to the responsible operator and follows the assigned response. Adding fluid or changing circulation is the operator's controlled task.

Changed application: no loss is reported, but flow continues unexpectedly after the planned pump stop. Do not dismiss it because the last density sample was correct. Record the observed behavior and alert the responsible person; do not conduct an unauthorized flow test to prove the point.

lessons.title: Q79-06 — Recognizing signals without explaining them away
lessons.body:
## Q79-06 — Recognizing signals without explaining them away

Monitoring combines trends, current operations and equipment condition. Unexpected active-volume gain, a return-flow change or flow when it is not expected can be important warning signs. A sensor reading may also be affected by transfers, equipment problems or other operations. An alternative explanation is a hypothesis to check, not permission to suppress a warning. Awareness personnel must report promptly and leave operational diagnosis to the designated competent person.

Use a small balance to understand why communication matters. Start with 80 bbl in the classroom active tank. A documented addition is 3 bbl and there are no other planned transfers. Expected volume is 83 bbl. The display reads 87 bbl, leaving 4 bbl unexplained. Report the actual reading, expected addition and difference. Do not call the unexplained amount a confirmed influx solely from this arithmetic. Equally, do not call it harmless because some addition occurred.

When making a report, include identity, well/location, time, observed change, ongoing operation and any known transfer. Ask for acknowledgment. If the primary contact does not respond, use the site's escalation route. A radio message that was transmitted but not received is not a completed handover. Do not enter a hazardous area to read a gauge more closely.

Worked message: 'This is the tank observer at training well W79. At 10:04 the active display is 87 bbl. We started at 80 and the recorded addition is 3. I have 4 bbl unexplained. Please acknowledge.' This states evidence without pretending to know the cause.

Changed application: maintenance says the display may be faulty, but there is also an unexpected flow observation. Keep both observations in the report. A suspected sensor fault does not invalidate an independent indication. Avoid repeated polling that delays the required alarm or protective action.

lessons.title: Q79-07 — Containment equipment and evidence of readiness
lessons.body:
## Q79-07 — Containment equipment and evidence of readiness

Pressure-control equipment is a system with components, connections, controls, energy supply, procedures and trained people. A blowout preventer can support containment under its designed conditions. An annular element and different ram arrangements have different capabilities. A device suitable for one pipe condition is not automatically suitable for another. A shear capability, for example, cannot be assumed for every item passing through the stack.

A choke provides controlled restriction in an appropriate flow path; an accumulator stores energy for hydraulic operation. Do not assume a choke will automatically solve a kick or that a closed-command indicator proves the barrier achieved its intended state. Function, position and integrity are different kinds of evidence. A pressure test, function test and visual inspection answer different questions, and each requires defined acceptance criteria.

At awareness level, ask whether the required equipment and current verification are confirmed by the responsible person. Do not perform a test, alter a valve alignment or operate an emergency control outside your authorization. If you are assigned an emergency action, it must be covered by site-specific instruction and competence, not by the fact that this course mentioned the component.

Worked situation: the control panel shows 'close command sent' while the response indication is unavailable. Report the discrepancy. Do not write 'barrier closed and verified' on the handover. The supervisor must use the approved response to establish the actual condition.

Changed application: a pressure-test certificate is valid for a similar stack with another equipment identifier. That is not proof for this assembly. Match the identification, configuration, test conditions and current acceptance record. The course does not supply universal test pressures, intervals or equipment ratings; these must come from the applicable program and competent technical authority.

lessons.title: Q79-08 — Intervention and workover awareness
lessons.body:
## Q79-08 — Intervention and workover awareness

Existing wells need investigation, maintenance and repair as well as drilling. An intervention may convey instruments or tools into a well, restore access, remove restrictions or support changes to production. A workover may involve more extensive changes to the completion. The boundary between terms varies with the job and organization; the actual equipment and pressure exposure matter more than the label.

Recognize wireline as a way to convey tools on a line, coiled tubing as continuous small-diameter tubing used for conveyance and/or circulation, and jointed tubing as connected pipe sections. Some operations intentionally retain well pressure while moving equipment through pressure-control arrangements. That requires a designed system and qualified crew. 'No drilling' and 'routine service' do not mean no well-control risk.

Before an intervention, the responsible team establishes the current well condition, intended flow paths, barriers, equipment compatibility and emergency responsibilities. An ancillary worker should understand the exclusion zones and communicate a change that could affect the operation. A service company's familiar equipment does not replace the well owner's current information. Simultaneous activities can affect access, ignition control, communication and response.

Worked situation: a wireline crew is ready to start, but the site briefing describes yesterday's pumping operation. A newcomer should request the current briefing and confirm the responsible contact. Entering because the crew looks experienced transfers an unresolved interface into the work area.

Changed application: a tubing replacement job is described as minor maintenance. Ask what pressure boundary will be opened and which competent person has confirmed the controls. Do not classify the job as low risk solely by its duration. The awareness learner remains outside live pressure-control manipulation and tool deployment.

lessons.title: Q79-09 — Pressure boundaries during intervention
lessons.body:
## Q79-09 — Pressure boundaries during intervention

An intervention pressure-control arrangement must contain pressure while allowing the intended operation. Equipment may include a lubricator to contain a tool assembly, sealing elements around a moving line or tubing, valves and emergency closure provisions. Exact arrangements depend on the conveyance, well conditions and approved procedure. A drawing used for awareness is not an installation specification.

Opening a pressure-containing connection is a distinct exposure. A gauge reading zero is not complete proof that every trapped section is depressurized or isolated. A blocked sensing path, isolated pocket or different pressure source may remain. Only the competent crew using the approved isolation and verification procedure establishes that it is safe to open. Awareness personnel should never loosen a fitting to 'see whether it is still pressured.'

Equipment ratings must be appropriate for the actual service, including pressure, temperature, fluid and configuration. Matching a nominal pressure number alone is inadequate. Seals, line sizes, tool dimensions and emergency closure compatibility are technical matters for the authorized team. A missing equipment record or changed component is information to resolve before relying on the system.

Worked situation: a line-conveyance assembly has been changed after the briefing. The new component has an unreadable identification plate. Report the change and missing traceability. A confident verbal claim that it is the same size does not establish suitability or approved configuration.

Changed application: a gauge reads zero after shutdown, and someone asks a new worker to loosen a union. The safe response is to refuse the unverified opening, keep clear and refer the task to the competent isolation team. The worker may assist only within a specifically authorized role after the controls are established. A completed awareness certificate is not that authorization.

lessons.title: Q79-10 — Emergency communication, muster and safe handover
lessons.body:
## Q79-10 — Emergency communication, muster and safe handover

An emergency response begins with the site's alarm and role instructions. Recognize the signal, stop your own unsafe exposure, notify through the designated channel and move or remain where the plan directs. Do not approach a release, search for a leak by smell or attempt rescue into a hazardous atmosphere without the required specialist team and equipment. Gas may present flammability, toxicity or oxygen-displacement hazards; absence of odor cannot establish safety.

Muster is an accountability process, not simply standing somewhere away from equipment. Use the assigned route and location unless the emergency instructions require an alternative. Report your identity and any known missing person information. Do not leave the site, return for belongings or self-dispatch to look for a colleague without authorization. A blocked route must be reported and the designated alternative used; do not improvise a path through the hazard.

After a concern, do not assume that silence means all-clear. Restart and re-entry require the responsible authority under the site procedure. Handover must preserve unresolved facts, actions taken, acknowledgments and restrictions. Say 'cause not established' where appropriate. A clean narrative that deletes uncertainty deprives the next team of information.

Worked integrated example: a volume discrepancy is reported during an operation change. The supervisor acknowledges, and an alarm then requires muster. The learner follows the muster route and reports at the register. They do not stay by the tank to collect a better trend. Later the handover records the discrepancy, time, known addition, acknowledgment and muster action; it does not state that an influx was confirmed unless authorized investigation established it.

Changed application: a colleague says the alarm is probably a drill and asks you to keep working. Follow the alarm instruction until an authorized announcement says otherwise. The same disciplined response protects people in a real event and makes a drill meaningful. The final outcome of this course is a person who recognizes, reports and acts within role—not a person authorized to control a well.

---

courses.title: VUC079 | VUC079 workbook, delivery and credential rules

content.title: VUC079 | VUC079 workbook, delivery and credential rules
content.description: Course completion records study only. Certification also requires the separately controlled examination and applicable observed assessments specified in the program. This VNDRLY/U curriculum counterpart does not award, replace, or claim accreditation by the external credential issuer.

lessons.title: VUC079 workbook, delivery and credential rules
lessons.body: # VUC079 workbook, delivery and credential rules

lessons.title: Delivery plan and materials
lessons.body:
## Delivery plan and materials

Planned learning time: 12 hours excluding breaks. Use 4 hours for ten chapters and demonstrations; 2 hours for four guided labs; 2.5 hours for the ten individual stations including changed tasks; 1 hour for the integrated role-play; 1 hour for the controlled final; 1.5 hours for feedback, correction and individual review. Adjust pacing for access needs without reducing outcomes. Additional remediation and reassessment may require another session.

Instructor must be competent in well-control principles and aware of the boundary between awareness and operational training. A person with current drilling/intervention competence should review locally adapted examples. No live well, pressure test, energized machinery, gas release, emergency equipment actuation or genuine alarm is needed or permitted in this course. All messages are simulated and prefixed TRAINING. Use paper diagrams, a calculator, printed cards and an unconnected mock radio. Never transmit an exercise onto an operational emergency channel.

Before class, print the coursebook, learning checks and this workbook for each learner. Print role/data cards R79 through M79 below. Keep final forms and answer keys separate; controlled files are in the private instructor directory. Provide large print or accessible digital text and read questions aloud when needed without explaining answers during assessment. Offer unit/arithmetic instruction before assessment. No visual-only or hearing-only alarm cue: provide equivalent textual and spoken cues. A role-play is not evidence of actual equipment-operating competence.

### D79 classroom drawing

A active tank → B pump → C drillpipe ↓ D bit → E annulus ↑ F solids processing → A tank.

Site board: well W79 and rig equipment inside a restricted zone. Visitor reception is outside. A mock supervisor contact is Radio 1; if unanswered, contact the exercise control lead at Radio 2. Real sites must supply their own channels, alarm meanings and competent roles. Diagram is a conventional classroom circuit, not a field valve lineup.

### Reusable forms

Observation: learner___ well/location___ time___ operation___ observed value/behavior___ expected basis___ known transfer___ uncertainty___ person contacted___ acknowledgment___ escalation___ protective action___ unresolved issue___ next responsible person___.

Barrier inquiry: well/equipment identifier___ drawing revision___ current operation___ intended containment path___ component claimed___ evidence offered___ mismatch/missing information___ restriction___ competent reviewer___ disposition___. This is an awareness inquiry, not an approved barrier certificate.

Station record: learner___ station___ first task evidence___ changed task evidence___ understanding__/2 observation/reasoning__/2 communication/role__/2 critical error Y/N___ assistance given___ result___ remediation___ reassessment variant/date___ assessor signature___.

lessons.title: W79-01 — Build the well story
lessons.body:
## W79-01 — Build the well story

Materials: seven lifecycle cards listed in P79-02; D79; blank barrier inquiry. Arrange the cards and explain where intervention can recur. Draw a pressure source, intended route and surface people. Use B79 with the missing plug verification. Write a question to the supervisor rather than inventing acceptance. Facilitator answer: lifecycle includes repeated work; a drawing alone does not verify a barrier; uncertain status stays visible. Changed case supplies a record for W80. Expected answer: resolve the identity mismatch. Accept a defensible alternative lifecycle sequence when the learner explains the actual work, not a memorized single order.

lessons.title: W79-02 — Calculate and challenge a model
lessons.body:
## W79-02 — Calculate and challenge a model

Use H79 and show formula, inputs, units and result. First calculate 10 ppg × 4,000 ft × 0.052 = 2,080 psi. Deliberately substitute measured depth 5,000 ft to obtain 2,600 psi and explain why it is wrong for this head. Reduce vertical height by 500 ft: 1,820 psi, 260 psi reduction. Changed case: 11 ppg at 3,000 ft gives 1,716 psi; at 2,800 ft gives 1,601.6. Ask whether any value authorizes work. Answer: no; formation/dynamic/approved-envelope information is absent. Facilitator must correct the tempting error of making the fluid heavier without authority.

lessons.title: W79-03 — Report the unexplained part
lessons.body:
## W79-03 — Report the unexplained part

Use V79 and mock radio. One learner is observer; the instructor is supervisor. Initial volume 80, addition 3, display 87 gives expected 83 and unexplained 4 bbl. Observer reports time, operation, identity and uncertainty. Instructor first says 'There was an addition.' Learner explains that the known addition was already included. Then instructor acknowledges and gives a simulated protective instruction. Learner repeats the instruction and follows it. Changed practice: start 70, confirmed addition 4, display 76 gives expected 74 and 2 unexplained. A faulty-sensor suggestion does not resolve a separate flow observation. Each learner performs individually, not through a group spokesperson.

lessons.title: W79-04 — Intervention and emergency boundary
lessons.body:
## W79-04 — Intervention and emergency boundary

Combine J79 and O79. Learner explains why an existing well can be pressured during service, asks for the current briefing and declines unverified opening despite a zero gauge. Introduce M79 and have the learner trace the safe alternate route on paper. Report at muster B and provide only known missing-person information. Changed case: normal route open, but a colleague proposes returning for a phone before all-clear. Follow the plan and do not return. Debrief the difference between helpful reporting and unauthorized technical intervention or rescue.

lessons.title: Individual observed stations
lessons.body:
## Individual observed stations

All ten stations are observed document/communication exercises. None is live technical practice. Each has three dimensions scored 0 wrong/missing/unsafe, 1 safe but incomplete or prompted, 2 independently correct with explanation. Require at least 5/6 on each station, at least 1 in every dimension, and no critical error. Learner performs the changed task too; score the weaker of initial/changed performance in each dimension so a rehearsed answer cannot conceal a gap. Stop an unsafe proposed action and mark the critical error. Re-teach then assess a genuinely changed variant on a later attempt; do not coach a passing attempt. Record verbatim behavior rather than 'seemed confident.'

### P79-01 — Role and report

Task/card: Use card R79: delivery worker sees an intermittent liquid release near well W79; substance unknown. Explain your role and make a report.

Observable criteria: Keep clear; report location/time/observation/uncertainty; obtain acknowledgment or escalate.

Changed task: Release stops before reply.

Changed criteria: Retain the observation and do not declare the condition safe.

Record scores and evidence on the reusable station form.

### P79-02 — Lifecycle and barrier evidence

Task/card: Use cards: planning, drilling, completion, production, intervention, suspension, abandonment. Arrange a plausible life cycle and inspect record B79: plug shown; verification blank.

Observable criteria: Explain recurring intervention; identify the missing verification; refer current status to the responsible person.

Changed task: Record supplied names well W80 rather than W79.

Changed criteria: Reject identity mismatch without inventing a barrier status.

Record scores and evidence on the reusable station form.

### P79-03 — Rig circuit and access

Task/card: Use diagram D79 below. Trace the conventional circuit and identify the controlled access boundary.

Observable criteria: Trace tank-pump-drillpipe-bit-annulus-processing-tank; name moving-pipe/pressure hazards; request actual induction.

Changed task: Assigned installation is floating; map supplied is for a land site.

Changed criteria: Request installation-specific route/alarm information before entry.

Record scores and evidence on the reusable station form.

### P79-04 — Static head interpretation

Task/card: Use calculator and model sheet H79:10 ppg; 4,000 vertical ft; 5,000 measured ft; then 500 vertical ft level loss.

Observable criteria: Show 2,080 psi initial, 1,820 remaining, 260 reduction; explain vertical height and model limit.

Changed task: 11 ppg; 3,000 vertical ft, then 200 ft level loss.

Changed criteria: Show 1,716 and 1,601.6 psi, reduction 114.4; do not prescribe a real density.

Record scores and evidence on the reusable station form.

### P79-05 — Influx recognition

Task/card: Card K79: recent acceptable density; reported losses; uncertain liquid level. Explain the issue.

Observable criteria: Explain that density alone does not establish full-column head; report and follow assigned response.

Changed task: Unexpected flow is observed after planned pump stop.

Changed criteria: Preserve the new cue and escalate without unauthorized testing.

Record scores and evidence on the reusable station form.

### P79-06 — Volume report

Task/card: Card V79: initial 80 bbl; confirmed addition 3; observed 87. Make a radio report to instructor as supervisor.

Observable criteria: Calculate expected 83 and unexplained 4; give well/time/operation and request acknowledgment.

Changed task: Instructor gives no acknowledgment; independent flow cue arrives.

Changed criteria: Use printed escalation route and report both cues; no hazardous investigation.

Record scores and evidence on the reusable station form.

### P79-07 — Equipment evidence

Task/card: Card E79: close command sent; feedback unavailable; test certificate says stack S80 while present stack is S79.

Observable criteria: Distinguish command/achieved state/integrity; identify equipment mismatch; report both.

Changed task: Feedback says closed but integrity evidence remains unavailable.

Changed criteria: Do not equate position alone with complete verification.

Record scores and evidence on the reusable station form.

### P79-08 — Intervention briefing

Task/card: Card J79: today line-conveyed tools; yesterday pumping; old briefing offered. Explain the preparation needed.

Observable criteria: Identify retained pressure possibility and current controls/roles/exclusion information.

Changed task: Job becomes tubing replacement described as minor.

Changed criteria: Judge actual pressure-boundary change, not label or duration.

Record scores and evidence on the reusable station form.

### P79-09 — Opening pressure boundaries

Task/card: Card O79: zero gauge; request to loosen a union; isolation confirmation absent. Role-play the response.

Observable criteria: Refuse unverified opening; keep clear; seek competent isolation/verification under procedure.

Changed task: New gauge again reads zero but a trapped section remains unresolved.

Changed criteria: Maintain the boundary; no experimental loosening.

Record scores and evidence on the reusable station form.

### P79-10 — Emergency and handover

Task/card: Card M79: alarm requires muster A via route North; release blocks North; printed plan designates route West to alternate muster B.

Observable criteria: Use West to B; identify yourself; report blocked route and known missing-person facts.

Changed task: Colleague says probably a drill; no authorized all-clear.

Changed criteria: Remain in the required accountability process; no unauthorized return or rescue.

Record scores and evidence on the reusable station form.

lessons.title: I79 — Integrated awareness handover
lessons.body:
## I79 — Integrated awareness handover

Purpose: demonstrate that a learner can connect an observation to safe communication and accountability. Instructor controls all cards; learner is an ancillary observer, never the well operator. Use a paper location board, mock radio, observation form and muster register. The technical supervisor role is played by the instructor. No valve action, kill calculation or real emergency call is requested.

Practice sequence: (1) W79 is changing from pumping to intervention; learner asks for current briefing. (2) Active volume is 80 bbl with 3 added and display 87; learner reports 4 unexplained. (3) Supervisor says the addition explains it; learner respectfully repeats that the addition is already accounted for. (4) Independent unexpected flow is reported. Learner adds it without declaring a proven cause. (5) Alarm requires muster; North is blocked and plan designates West to B. Learner follows the alternate and reports identity. (6) One colleague is absent; learner reports last known facts without self-dispatching a search. (7) No all-clear exists; learner rejects a request to return for records. (8) Learner completes a handover with unresolved cause and authority boundary.

Practice debrief: good performance is not a diagnosis of an actual kick. It is accurate evidence, prompt acknowledged escalation, protective behavior and truthful handover. Do not let arithmetic delay an immediate alarm if the scenario gives an obvious hazard first.

Independent assessment variant A: well W179; starting tank 100 bbl; confirmed addition 4; observed 107; current job is line-conveyed tools. Correct balance is expected 104 and 3 unexplained. Primary supervisor initially does not respond; use the printed backup. After acknowledgment, introduce independent flow and an alarm. North is available; muster A applies. A colleague says the event is probably a drill. Require compliance and a truthful handover.

Changed reassessment variant B: well W279; start 60 bbl; confirmed addition 2; display 67. Correct balance is expected 62 and 5 unexplained. Supervisor acknowledges but says the display may be faulty. Introduce independent flow, blocked North and designated West/B. A colleague requests return before all-clear. Learner must preserve both observations, follow the alternate, remain accountable and document uncertainty.

Integrated rubric: six dimensions (current briefing/role, evidence balance, acknowledged escalation, independent-cue treatment, safe muster/accountability, truthful handover), each 0 unsafe/missing, 1 substantially prompted, 2 safe but incomplete, 3 independently correct, 4 correct and clearly explains limitations. Require 20/24 with every dimension at least 3 and no critical error. Dangerous approach/opening, suppressing an unresolved warning, unauthorized equipment manipulation, disregarding the alarm, unauthorized rescue or fabricated verification is a critical failure. Individual result only; no group credit. Learner___ variant___ six scores___ critical issue___ evidence quotations___ outcome___ assessor/date___.

lessons.title: Final, remediation and award
lessons.body:
## Final, remediation and award

Final Form A contains ten cases with three scored decisions each: 60 points, 60 minutes, pass 48/60 and at least 4/6 in every domain with no unresolved critical error. Each decision scores 2 correct with sound reason, 1 safe but incomplete, 0 incorrect/missing/unsafe. Coursebook/calculator allowed; keys, other people and outside assistance prohibited. A changed Form B is reserved for reassessment and includes the original context plus the changed task. Assess only the changed task's three decisions. Reasoning and safe limits matter more than matching exact words. Do not round a failed criterion upward.

For an error, identify the exact chapter and behavior, explain the misconception, require a corrected worked example and a changed application. Reassess only after the instructor establishes readiness; repeat all failed stations and the integrated exercise when a critical behavior affected it. Final reassessment uses the complete changed form to preserve the breadth of evidence. If further attempts are needed, an instructor prepares and reviews a genuinely new equivalent form; do not repeatedly expose the same answer key.

Issue 'VNDRLY/U Well Control Awareness' only after all chapters and 20 checks are corrected, ten stations pass, integrated exercise passes and final passes. Retain identity, version/hash, attendance, adjustments, scored papers, individual observations, remediation and assessor/date. A written-only learner receives a record of learning, not this complete award. Certificate lists awareness scope and expressly excludes IWCF accreditation and operational authorization. No external exam or certificate is awarded by this package.

VNDRLY administrative review interval: two years, or earlier after a significant role/procedure change, incident or demonstrated gap. This is an internal training rule, not a claim about IWCF certificate expiry or a regulatory interval. Site induction and task-specific competence remain necessary. Learner may appeal a result to a second competent assessor using retained evidence; protect exam keys and personal records. Never amend an original score without preserving the correction and reason.


---

courses.title: VUC079 | VUC079 formative checks

content.title: VUC079 | VUC079 formative checks
content.description: Course completion records study only. Certification also requires the separately controlled examination and applicable observed assessments specified in the program. This VNDRLY/U curriculum counterpart does not award, replace, or claim accreditation by the external credential issuer.

lessons.title: VUC079 formative checks
lessons.body:
# VUC079 formative checks

Attempt before reading the explanation. Correct errors and revisit the matching chapter/station. These are not the controlled final.

lessons.title: Q79-01-L1
lessons.body:
## Q79-01-L1

A driver sees a clear liquid escaping near a wellhead. What should the driver report?

**Answer:** The location, time and observed escape, with the fluid identity unknown; remain clear and notify the designated contact.

**Reason/remediation:** Appearance is not reliable identification and investigation must not create exposure. Revisit Q79-01 and perform its changed application.

lessons.title: Q79-01-L2
lessons.body:
## Q79-01-L2

The escape stops. Is reporting still useful?

**Answer:** Yes. Preserve the observation and timing even when the symptom is intermittent.

**Reason/remediation:** Disappearance of a symptom is not proof that its cause was removed. Revisit Q79-01 and perform its changed application.

lessons.title: Q79-02-L1
lessons.body:
## Q79-02-L1

A suspended well drawing shows a plug, but verification is blank. Can the plug be counted as verified?

**Answer:** No. Resolve the missing evidence with the responsible supervisor before relying on it.

**Reason/remediation:** A planned component and a verified barrier are different. Revisit Q79-02 and perform its changed application.

lessons.title: Q79-02-L2
lessons.body:
## Q79-02-L2

What must a handover identify beyond the well name?

**Answer:** Current operation and configuration, barrier status, unresolved issues, restrictions and responsible contact.

**Reason/remediation:** The receiving team needs the present condition, not merely historical equipment names. Revisit Q79-02 and perform its changed application.

lessons.title: Q79-03-L1
lessons.body:
## Q79-03-L1

Trace the classroom conventional circulation circuit A tank, B pump, C drillpipe, D bit, E annulus, F solids processing.

**Answer:** A-B-C-D-E-F-A.

**Reason/remediation:** Returns rise through the annulus in this particular conventional model. Revisit Q79-03 and perform its changed application.

lessons.title: Q79-03-L2
lessons.body:
## Q79-03-L2

Does a land-rig induction establish offshore muster arrangements?

**Answer:** No. Obtain the actual installation briefing and emergency routes.

**Reason/remediation:** Different environments and configurations require their own instructions. Revisit Q79-03 and perform its changed application.

lessons.title: Q79-04-L1
lessons.body:
## Q79-04-L1

Calculate the static pressure for 10 ppg and 4,000 ft vertical height.

**Answer:** 2,080 psi: 0.052 × 10 × 4,000.

**Reason/remediation:** The units and vertical head are part of the model; this is not a field operating limit. Revisit Q79-04 and perform its changed application.

lessons.title: Q79-04-L2
lessons.body:
## Q79-04-L2

The same column loses 500 ft of liquid height. Find the remaining head and reduction.

**Answer:** 1,820 psi remaining and 260 psi reduction.

**Reason/remediation:** Use 3,500 ft remaining height; a suitable density does not compensate for an unfilled column. Revisit Q79-04 and perform its changed application.

lessons.title: Q79-05-L1
lessons.body:
## Q79-05-L1

Why can a correct density sample fail to prove safety while fluid is being lost?

**Answer:** The fluid column may no longer be full and pressure can decrease.

**Reason/remediation:** Density is only one input; head and changing conditions also matter. Revisit Q79-05 and perform its changed application.

lessons.title: Q79-05-L2
lessons.body:
## Q79-05-L2

Why report unexpected flow even when the last static calculation looked adequate?

**Answer:** A real observation may indicate conditions outside that simplified calculation.

**Reason/remediation:** Dynamic effects and uncertain inputs can invalidate reassurance based only on static arithmetic. Revisit Q79-05 and perform its changed application.

lessons.title: Q79-06-L1
lessons.body:
## Q79-06-L1

Start 80 bbl, documented addition 3 bbl, display 87 bbl. Calculate the unexplained difference and response.

**Answer:** Expected 83 bbl; 4 bbl unexplained. Report immediately with the known addition and actual observation.

**Reason/remediation:** Do not hide the discrepancy or claim its cause is proven by arithmetic alone. Revisit Q79-06 and perform its changed application.

lessons.title: Q79-06-L2
lessons.body:
## Q79-06-L2

A suspect display and independent unexpected flow are reported. May the flow be dismissed?

**Answer:** No. Report both and follow the designated response.

**Reason/remediation:** One potentially faulty source does not invalidate an independent observation. Revisit Q79-06 and perform its changed application.

lessons.title: Q79-07-L1
lessons.body:
## Q79-07-L1

Is close command sent the same as barrier closure verified?

**Answer:** No. State the command and the missing achieved-state evidence separately.

**Reason/remediation:** A command, a position indication and integrity confirmation answer different questions. Revisit Q79-07 and perform its changed application.

lessons.title: Q79-07-L2
lessons.body:
## Q79-07-L2

A test record names a different assembly. Is that enough?

**Answer:** No. Resolve identity/configuration and verification for this assembly.

**Reason/remediation:** Similar equipment is not the same traceable equipment. Revisit Q79-07 and perform its changed application.

lessons.title: Q79-08-L1
lessons.body:
## Q79-08-L1

Why can a routine wireline job need pressure-control planning?

**Answer:** It accesses an existing well that may retain pressure and uses a specific containment arrangement.

**Reason/remediation:** The absence of drilling does not remove the pressure source. Revisit Q79-08 and perform its changed application.

lessons.title: Q79-08-L2
lessons.body:
## Q79-08-L2

Yesterday’s pumping briefing is offered for today’s tubing job. What is missing?

**Answer:** The current operation, pressure boundaries, controls, exclusion zones and responsibilities.

**Reason/remediation:** An outdated briefing can omit the actual interfaces and hazards. Revisit Q79-08 and perform its changed application.

lessons.title: Q79-09-L1
lessons.body:
## Q79-09-L1

A zero gauge is offered as the sole reason to loosen a union. What should the learner do?

**Answer:** Do not open it; keep clear and refer to the competent isolation and verification process.

**Reason/remediation:** Other trapped pressure or a sensing problem may remain. Revisit Q79-09 and perform its changed application.

lessons.title: Q79-09-L2
lessons.body:
## Q79-09-L2

A replacement component has no readable identity. How should an awareness worker respond?

**Answer:** Report the change and unresolved suitability/traceability; do not approve it.

**Reason/remediation:** Nominal size or appearance cannot establish its rating, service compatibility or authorization. Revisit Q79-09 and perform its changed application.

lessons.title: Q79-10-L1
lessons.body:
## Q79-10-L1

An alarm sounds and a colleague calls it probably a drill. What governs?

**Answer:** Follow the site alarm and muster instructions until an authorized all-clear or other direction.

**Reason/remediation:** Speculation must not replace the response plan. Revisit Q79-10 and perform its changed application.

lessons.title: Q79-10-L2
lessons.body:
## Q79-10-L2

Can the learner return to the tank to improve the event log after muster starts?

**Answer:** No. Follow muster/accountability; report the known observations from safety.

**Reason/remediation:** Data collection must not override emergency protection. Revisit Q79-10 and perform its changed application.

## Verification boundary

Full original instruction, examples, explained checks, four labs, ten observed classroom stations, integrated practice/A/B variants, protected written A/B forms and keys, instructor rules and credential records are included. These materials do not provide an operational well-control qualification, an equipment test specification, a live-well drill, a rescue qualification or a legal compliance opinion. Actual operations require the relevant current approved program, equipment instructions, competent personnel and site-specific authorization. Those boundaries are teaching outcomes, not missing live exercises for an awareness award.

Public pages were checked for topic relevance and material distinctions. Proprietary learning screens and external exam items were not copied or claimed reviewed. Original fictional quantities are independently checked in verification-results.json. No real company or well records are used.

lessons.title: VNDRLY/U International Industry Safety Foundations
lessons.body:
# VNDRLY/U International Industry Safety Foundations

VUC080 · Original materials · 18 November 2026

This program addresses the nine public IMIST topic families for new industry entrants and workers needing a broad safety foundation. It is a VNDRLY award, not an OPITO-approved IMIST certificate or a Vantage registration. No prerequisite qualification is required; accessible reading/arithmetic support is available. Completion does not qualify specialist work, replace site induction or establish offshore medical fitness.

Outcomes: recognize hazards; make a factual observation; participate in risk assessment and control of work; report integrity issues; plan benign handling; interpret substance controls; recognize fall and lifting exposures. Demonstrations are classroom or ground-level only.

lessons.title: Q80-01 — Recognize the hazardous environment
lessons.body:
## Q80-01 — Recognize the hazardous environment

Energy sites combine process hazards with everyday work hazards. A pressurized hydrocarbon system can release fuel; an ignition source can turn a release into a fire or explosion. A toxic or oxygen-deficient atmosphere may harm people without a visible flame. Vehicles, moving equipment, electrical energy, noise, weather and work near water can cause injury even when the process is operating normally. A major accident can affect many people and systems; a personal injury event can affect one person. Both deserve prevention, but low injury numbers do not prove major-accident barriers are healthy.

Before beginning work, locate the actual work area, access restrictions, emergency signal, reporting route and assembly point. Identify what could reach you from nearby work: a swinging load, a vehicle route, a release, falling objects or another crew's test. Remote sites also require planning for communication and medical response. A familiar job at an unfamiliar installation is not automatically familiar work.

Ask three questions: what energy or substance could cause harm, how could I or someone else be exposed, and what verified control prevents that exposure? 'Be careful' is not a physical barrier. A painted line alone does not stop a vehicle; a warning sign alone does not contain pressure. Controls must fit the actual hazard and remain effective as the work changes.

Worked case: a worker is sent to read a label beside a pipe rack. The route passes below a lifting operation, and a nearby leak alarm has activated. The worker should not treat the quick duration as permission to enter. Remain outside the affected zone, notify the responsible contact and follow the emergency direction. Getting the label can wait; exposure cannot be undone.

Changed case: the alarm clears, but the lifting exclusion remains. Do not assume all restrictions ended together. Confirm the status of each relevant control. This course teaches recognition and safe participation; it does not qualify the learner for rescue, gas testing or process shutdown duties.

lessons.title: Q80-02 — Work safely and report useful observations
lessons.body:
## Q80-02 — Work safely and report useful observations

A safety management system links responsibilities, planning, competence, work procedures, emergency arrangements, reporting and improvement. A site-specific system should tell you who controls the work and how to raise a concern. Where a safety-case approach applies, the duty holder demonstrates how major hazards are managed; an individual worker still needs practical instructions for today's task. Different jurisdictions use different legal arrangements. Do not assume a rule from one country is the universal legal requirement everywhere.

You contribute by using the agreed method, checking your understanding, reporting changes and refusing work outside your competence or controls. Supervisors and employers must provide the conditions and resources for safe work; safety is not transferred entirely to the last person holding a tool. Fatigue, language, workload and conflicting instructions can undermine a good procedure. Raise those conditions early rather than hiding them to appear capable.

A useful observation describes the task, location, condition, potential harm, immediate protection and requested follow-up. It focuses on evidence, not blame. Report a near miss even when nobody was injured. Record a positive control when it genuinely prevented exposure, but do not use a quota of positive cards to suppress a serious concern. After reporting, know who owns the action and how closure will be verified.

Worked observation: 'At access lane B at 09:10, stored pallets obscured the marked pedestrian crossing. A forklift was approaching. I stayed outside the lane and contacted the area supervisor. Please restore a protected pedestrian route before access resumes.' This is more actionable than 'operator careless.' It identifies the condition and the control needed.

Changed case: a supervisor says the pallets have always been there. Explain the present exposure and seek the site escalation route if unresolved. Do not cross to prove the hazard. An observation card is not a substitute for an immediate warning when someone is in danger. Preserve factual records, including disagreement and acknowledgment, without adding accusations.

lessons.title: Q80-03 — Assess risk and verify controls
lessons.body:
## Q80-03 — Assess risk and verify controls

Hazard identification asks what can harm people; risk assessment considers the exposure, possible consequence and likelihood under actual conditions. Break a job into steps, identify who may be affected, select controls, assign responsibility and verify that controls exist before starting. Include maintenance staff, contractors, visitors and nearby crews rather than only the person performing the central task.

Prefer eliminating the hazardous task or exposure where feasible. If it remains, consider safer methods or substances, engineered separation, administrative arrangements and suitable personal protective equipment. PPE can be necessary but does not make a failed primary control acceptable. Controls can interact: a screen that contains debris may obstruct an escape route, and ventilation can carry a contaminant toward another workgroup.

A risk matrix is a decision aid, not a measurement of safety. This course's fictional matrix uses likelihood 1 unlikely, 2 possible, 3 likely, and severity 1 minor, 2 serious, 3 potentially fatal. Multiply to prioritize discussion only. For the classroom, any missing critical control means HOLD regardless of score. A reduction in likelihood must have a reason supported by an implemented control, not simply a lower number written to obtain approval.

Worked case: a person could be struck by a moving load, likelihood 2 and severity 3: score 6. A verified exclusion and controlled route may reduce the fictional likelihood to 1, score 3; the potential severity remains 3. If the exclusion is removed, the lower score no longer has its basis. The job must be reassessed and the exposure controlled, not continued because the form was signed earlier.

Changed case: weather reduces visibility during the lift. Stop the affected activity through the work-control process and reassess with the responsible team. A last-minute personal check is useful but cannot replace a formal assessment, competent lift plan or permit where required. Record residual concerns and the person authorized to accept them.

lessons.title: Q80-04 — Understand permits and the control of work
lessons.body:
## Q80-04 — Understand permits and the control of work

A permit-to-work system coordinates specified work under defined conditions. It identifies scope, location, equipment, responsible people, hazards, precautions, validity and handback. It is communication and authorization within the site's system, not a guarantee that every hazard has disappeared. Some work needs a permit because of its interfaces or energy exposure; the site's rules determine the categories and authorities.

Read the actual scope and limits before signing acceptance. Confirm that the work area and equipment identifiers match. Understand required isolations, tests, barriers and other linked permits. Do not sign for a check you did not perform or are not qualified to verify. A permit receiver and an isolation authority may have different responsibilities. A padlock or tag is not a complete explanation of the isolation boundary.

Work can become invalid when the task, crew, equipment, conditions or adjacent operations change. Follow suspension and revalidation rules. An alarm may require stopping and leaving the work area; a shift change may require a formal handover. Do not extend a validity time yourself or borrow a neighboring crew's permit. At completion, account for people, tools and condition, communicate incomplete work and obtain the required handback before equipment is returned to service.

Worked case: permit P80 covers cold inspection of pump A from 08:00 to 12:00. At 11:40 the crew proposes grinding a seized fastener. Grinding introduces a different activity and possible ignition source. The existing permit does not automatically cover it. Suspend the changed scope and refer to the issuing authority for assessment and authorization before proceeding.

Changed case: no grinding is needed, but the job continues past 12:00. The scope may be unchanged while authorization has expired. Stop and follow extension/reissue rules. A verbal 'nearly finished' does not alter the written control. Site-specific training is required before acting as an actual permit issuer, receiver or isolation specialist.

lessons.title: Q80-05 — Protect asset integrity
lessons.body:
## Q80-05 — Protect asset integrity

Asset integrity means equipment and supporting systems can perform their intended functions without unacceptable harm. It includes design, installation, operation, inspection, maintenance and controlled change. A safety-critical function may prevent an event or limit its consequences. Examples include containment, detection, shutdown, fire protection and escape arrangements. Some failures remain hidden until a demand occurs; apparently normal production is not evidence that every protective system works.

Workers support integrity by identifying equipment correctly, staying within operating instructions and reporting deterioration or abnormal behavior. A missing guard, damaged support, leak, blocked escape, overdue inspection or inhibited detector should not disappear into an informal assumption. Describe the condition and its possible effect, then use the designated defect process. Competent personnel decide repair, isolation, compensating measures and any permitted continued operation.

An impairment is not controlled merely because it is known. It needs an authorized decision, defined restrictions or alternative protection where appropriate, a responsible owner and a time/review condition. Do not bypass an alarm to stop nuisance messages or reset a trip repeatedly without understanding the cause. Unauthorized modification can remove a barrier for people who do not know it changed.

Worked case: detector D80 is shown as inhibited in the control record while hot work is proposed nearby. An observer cannot approve the combination. Report the impairment to the work-control authority and hold the affected work until the responsible team evaluates the combined condition. 'Maintenance already knows' does not resolve the permit interface.

Changed case: a repair work order is marked closed, but the physical guard is still missing. Report the mismatch and retain the restriction. Administrative closure and restored function are not identical. A completion record should reflect the actual equipment and evidence, not a desire to reduce the backlog.

lessons.title: Q80-06 — Plan manual handling rather than proving strength
lessons.body:
## Q80-06 — Plan manual handling rather than proving strength

Manual handling includes carrying, lifting, lowering, pushing, pulling and supporting a load. Injury risk depends on the task, load, person and environment, not only mass. A light awkward object carried repeatedly through a narrow route can be difficult. A wet grip, sharp edge, unstable contents, poor visibility or twisted posture can change the risk. There is no single kilogram value that makes every lift safe for everyone.

First ask whether the handling can be avoided or redesigned. Deliver closer to the point of use, reduce package size where appropriate, use a suitable handling aid, or change storage height and route. A team lift is not automatically safe: people need a coordinated method, adequate space and a stable load. Each participant must be able to stop. Do not infer safe team capacity by adding individual lifting limits.

For the benign training object, inspect the route and destination, assess the grip and balance, keep the object close where practicable, move smoothly and turn with the feet instead of twisting under load. Set down before adjusting an insecure grip. Stop if pain, loss of balance or unexpected weight occurs. Technique supplements risk reduction; it does not justify a poorly designed task.

Worked case: a sealed box weighs 18 kg, must be carried 40 m and blocks the worker's view. Its mass alone cannot establish safety. Consider a suitable trolley and clear route, delivery closer to use or smaller packages after assessing the contents. Do not ask the learner to prove the lift by trying it.

Changed case: the box is only 5 kg but has a hot surface and no secure handhold. The reduced mass does not remove those hazards. Arrange a safe method and appropriate equipment. Physical practice in this package uses only an empty lightweight training box, with individual consent and adjustments; no maximum-strength test is permitted.

lessons.title: Q80-07 — Control hazardous substances and exposure
lessons.body:
## Q80-07 — Control hazardous substances and exposure

Hazardous substances include purchased products and materials generated by work, such as dust, fume, mist or gas. Exposure can occur by breathing, skin or eye contact, swallowing contamination, or other task-specific routes. Harm can be immediate or develop after repeated exposure. A product's smell, familiar brand or small quantity cannot establish that its use is safe.

Read the correct label and current safety data sheet, then relate the information to the actual task. Identification, hazards, first aid, handling/storage, exposure controls and incompatibilities help inform the assessment. An SDS alone is not the task risk assessment. Spraying, heating or using a product in a confined area can create a different exposure from a small wipe application. Process-generated contaminants may have no purchased-product label.

Control exposure at source where practicable: avoid the substance or process, use a suitable safer alternative, enclose or capture emissions, and apply the assessed work method. PPE selection must match the substance and exposure; not every glove protects against every chemical, and a generic dust mask is not a universal respirator. Respiratory protection requires the appropriate program, selection, fit and training. Do not improvise chemical mixing or neutralization.

Worked case: an unlabeled bottle is offered as a cleaning product. The worker should not sniff or test it. Segregate/report it through the site's procedure and obtain correct identification and assessment before use. If a release occurs, follow the emergency instructions and only undertake cleanup within training and authorization.

Changed case: the correct product is identified, but local extraction is not working and the task has changed from wiping to spraying. The previous control assumptions no longer apply. Hold the changed task, report the failed control and obtain reassessment. The correct label does not make an ineffective exposure-control system acceptable.

lessons.title: Q80-08 — Recognize work-at-height and dropped-object risks
lessons.body:
## Q80-08 — Recognize work-at-height and dropped-object risks

A fall can injure a person even when the work is brief or relatively low. Edges, openings, fragile surfaces and access equipment all need consideration. The first question is whether the task can be done without exposure to a fall. If not, select suitable prevention and protection through competent planning. Collective protection such as a suitable guarded platform protects without relying solely on each person's attachment action.

A ladder, scaffold, mobile platform and personal fall system are not interchangeable. Selection depends on task, duration, access, surface, weather and rescue needs. Training in this awareness course does not authorize scaffold alteration, platform operation, anchorage selection or fall-arrest use. A harness alone is not a complete system; compatibility, clearance, anchorage, inspection and rescue arrangements matter.

Protect people below as well as those above. Tools and materials can fall or be displaced. Establish the required exclusion and secure items using an approved arrangement; do not improvise attachments that create other hazards. Maintain safe access and escape. A closed access gate or missing scaffold tag must be resolved through the site's competent process, not bypassed because the work will take a minute.

Worked case: a label can be photographed from ground level using a suitable remote method. This avoids climbing solely to read it. If a later task requires hands-on work, that is a new assessment, not permission inherited from the photograph job.

Changed case: a worker proposes standing on a box beside an unprotected opening. Stop the unsafe approach and obtain a suitable planned method. Do not teach a universal height threshold below which no precautions are needed; the possibility and consequences of a fall govern the assessment. In this course all diagrams and demonstrations remain at floor level.

lessons.title: Q80-09 — Stay safe around mechanical lifting
lessons.body:
## Q80-09 — Stay safe around mechanical lifting

Mechanical lifting moves a load with equipment such as a crane or hoist. Safe execution depends on a competent plan, suitable equipment, known load information, appropriate rigging, ground or support conditions, communication and exclusion of people from danger. An awareness learner should recognize these dependencies without pretending to be a lift planner, rigger or crane operator.

A suspended load can move, rotate or fall. Keep clear of the load path, pinch points and the space between a load and a fixed object. Never walk under a suspended load to save time. Do not catch or steady a moving load with your body. Tagline use, signaling and rigging tasks require specific instruction and authorization; a nearby worker should not spontaneously take over a signaler's role.

Inspection tags and rated-capacity markings provide information but do not prove suitability for every arrangement. Sling angle, hitch, load distribution, center of gravity and attachment condition can affect the lift. Missing identification, damage or changed configuration must be referred to the competent lifting team. The absence of visible damage is not a complete inspection.

Worked case: a planned 900 kg load will use 100 kg of lifting accessories. For this fictional planning check, total suspended mass is 1,000 kg before any other items the actual plan must include. A worker who reports only the 900 kg item has omitted part of the load. That calculation alone does not approve a crane or sling; configuration and other requirements remain.

Changed case: the route is moved closer to a pedestrian walkway after the briefing. The old exclusion arrangement may no longer protect people. Stop the affected activity through the designated communication process and have the competent team reassess. Everyone can raise an immediate danger, but routine lifting signals and restart authority must remain clear. The integrated course exercise combines this interface with permits, chemicals and asset condition so learners practice recognizing conflicting controls.

---

content.description: Course completion records study only. Certification also requires the separately controlled examination and applicable observed assessments specified in the program.
